domain: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
title: Project vs Program vs Portfolio
summary: Projects, programs, and portfolios represent different levels of organizational work management, from individual initiatives to strategic alignment.
key_concepts: Project = temporary, unique deliverable
Program = group of related projects managed together
Portfolio = collection of projects/programs aligned with strategy
Operations = ongoing, repetitive work

project.definition: A sequence of unique, complex, and connected activities that have one goal or purpose and that must be completed by a specific time, within budget, and according to specification.
characteristics: Has a defined start and end
project.real world example: Build a warehouse system for a client

program.definition: A group of related projects managed in a coordinated way

portfolio.definition: A collection of projects/programs managed to achieve strategic goals

exam_tips: Project = tactical execution. Program = benefits. Portfolio = strategy alignment. Always distinguish clearly in exam questions.

domain: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
title: Project Objective
summary: Project objectives define what the project aims to achieve in measurable and specific terms.
key_concepts: Objectives must be SMART
Linked to business value
Defined early (charter phase)
Guide scope and success criteria
exam_tips: If objective is unclear → project risk increases. PMP prefers clear, measurable objectives linked to business value.

domain: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
title: Strategic Dependencies (Project – Program – Portfolio)
summary: Dependencies at project, program, and portfolio levels define how initiatives rely on each other to deliver value, benefits, and strategic alignment.
key_concepts: Projects can depend on other projects
Programs manage interdependencies between projects
Portfolios manage dependencies to optimize strategic value
Dependencies impact sequencing, risk, and resource allocation

project_level_dependency.definition: A project may rely on outputs, resources, or timing of another project
examples: Project B depends on Project A delivering a system first
Infrastructure project must complete before application rollout

program_level_dependency.definition: Program coordinates multiple related projects with strong interdependencies
examples: ERP implementation program: finance module depends on core system
Digital transformation with multiple integrated systems
impact: Delays in one project affect the entire program

portfolio_level_dependency.definition: Portfolio manages dependencies across projects/programs to align with strategy
examples: Investment prioritization based on dependency and ROI
Delay of one program impacts strategic roadmap

dependency_types.description: One initiative requires output of another
A capability must exist before another initiative starts
Alignment or sequencing driven by business strategy

exam_tips: Projects have dependencies. Programs MANAGE dependencies. Portfolios OPTIMIZE dependencies aligned with strategy.

domain: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
title: PMI Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct
summary: The PMI Code of Ethics defines the expected behavior of project management professionals through four core values: Responsibility, Respect, Fairness, and Honesty.
key_concepts: 4 Core Values: Responsibility, Respect, Fairness, Honesty
Applies to all PMI members and practitioners
Guides ethical decision-making
Important for exam situational questions

core_values.name: Responsibility
core_values.definition: Take ownership of decisions and actions
pm_application: Escalate issues instead of hiding them

core_values.name: Respect
core_values.definition: Show consideration for people and culture

core_values.name: Honesty
pm_application: Do not hide delays or issues

ethical_scenarios.scenario: Project delay but PM hides it
Selecting vendor based on personal relationship

exam_tips: If a scenario involves unethical behavior, ALWAYS choose transparency, accountability, and professional integrity. PMI strongly favors honesty and escalation over hiding issues.

domain: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
title: Constraints, Assumptions, and Risks
summary: Constraints, assumptions, and risks are key elements that influence project planning, execution, and uncertainty management.
key_concepts: Constraints limit project execution
Assumptions are treated as true without proof
Risks represent uncertainty (positive or negative)
All three impact planning and decision-making

constraints.definition: Limiting factors that affect the execution of a project

assumptions.definition: Factors considered to be true without proof for planning purposes
risks_associated: If assumption is wrong → becomes a risk

risks.definition: An uncertain event or condition that can have a positive or negative effect on project objectives

exam_tips: Assumptions create risk. Constraints limit options. Risks must be actively managed throughout the project lifecycle.

domain: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
title: Product, Product Life Cycle, and Project Life Cycle
summary: Products and projects operate on different lifecycles. Projects create products, while products evolve over a longer product life cycle.
key_concepts: Project creates product
Project life cycle is temporary
Product life cycle is long-term
Multiple projects can exist within one product life cycle

product.definition: A product is a tangible or intangible output that delivers value to customers or users.

product_lifecycle.definition: The full life span of a product from idea to retirement.
characteristics: Focused on value delivery and market performance
examples: A SaaS product evolving over years
Retail product from launch to phase-out

project_lifecycle.definition: The series of phases that a project passes through from initiation to closure.
examples: Build version 1 of a mobile app

relationships: Multiple projects can exist within one product life cycle
Product life cycle continues after project ends
Programs may manage multiple projects contributing to a product
exam_tips: Project life cycle is temporary. Product life cycle is long-term. A project delivers a product, but the product continues after the project ends.

domain: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
title: Working with OPAs and EEFs
summary: EEFs are environmental conditions that constrain or influence the project and cannot be controlled, while OPAs are internal organizational assets that can be used to support project work.
key_concepts: EEFs must be accepted and adapted to
OPAs can be used, reused, and sometimes updated
EEFs can be internal or external
OPAs are always internal

EEFs.definition: Conditions outside the direct control of the project manager that influence or constrain project execution.
characteristics: Can positively or negatively impact project

OPAs.definition: Organizational assets such as processes, templates, and knowledge repositories that support project execution.

exam_tips: EEFs = conditions you cannot control. OPAs = assets you can use. Policies are OPAs even if you must follow them.

domain: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
title: Project Development Approach
summary: A project development approach defines how project work is organized, planned, and executed to deliver outcomes. The main approaches include Predictive, Agile (Adaptive), and Hybrid.
key_concepts: Development approach determines how work is done
Three main types: Predictive, Agile, Hybrid
Choice depends on uncertainty, requirements stability, and environment
Approach influences planning, execution, and control

predictive.definition: A development approach where scope, schedule, and cost are defined early and changes are controlled.

agile.definition: An adaptive approach that delivers value through iterative and incremental work cycles, allowing continuous feedback and improvement.

iterative.definition: A development technique where the product is repeatedly refined and improved through multiple cycles.
characteristics: Feedback used to enhance product quality

incremental.definition: A development technique where the product is built and delivered in small, usable portions.
incremental.focus: Delivering new value step by step

agile.example: A product is developed through multiple iterations where the team continuously improves existing features while also delivering new features in increments.

hybrid.definition: A combination of predictive and agile approaches used together in a project.

exam_tips: Predictive = stable requirements. Agile = changing requirements. Hybrid = mix both depending on project context.

domain: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
title: Tailoring in Project Management
summary: Tailoring is the process of adapting project management approach, processes, and practices to fit the specific needs of a project.
key_concepts: No one-size-fits-all approach
Tailoring adapts methods to project context
Driven by project complexity, risk, and environment
Applies to both predictive and agile approaches

details.definition: The deliberate adjustment of project management processes, tools, and techniques to match the project's context and needs.
why tailoring: Projects differ in size, complexity, and risk

exam_tips: PMI always supports tailoring. The best approach is the one that fits the project, not strictly following all processes.

domain: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
title: Uncertainty and Complexity
summary: Uncertainty and complexity influence how projects are managed, requiring adaptive thinking, risk awareness, and appropriate development approaches.
key_concepts: Uncertainty relates to unknowns
Complexity comes from interactions and dependencies
Higher uncertainty drives agile approaches
Requires continuous assessment and adaptation

uncertainty.definition: A lack of clarity or predictability regarding project outcomes, requirements, or environment.

complexity.definition: The degree of interrelated parts, interactions, and dependencies that make a project difficult to manage.
impact: Need for strong communication and governance

exam_tips: High uncertainty = Agile. Low uncertainty = Predictive. Complexity increases the need for collaboration and adaptability.

domain: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
title: Project Governance
summary: Project governance is the framework of policies, processes, and structures that guide project decisions, ensure alignment, and provide oversight.
key_concepts: Governance provides direction and control
Ensures alignment with organizational strategy
Defines roles, responsibilities, and decision rights
Applies across project, program, and portfolio levels

details.definition: A structured framework that defines how projects are directed, controlled, and monitored.

exam_tips: Governance ensures control and alignment. It defines who makes decisions and how the project is monitored.

title: Predictive Approach — Overview
summary: The predictive (Waterfall) approach is a plan-driven methodology where project scope, schedule, and cost are defined upfront before execution begins. Work is performed in a sequential and structured manner.
key_concepts: Plan-driven approach with detailed upfront planning
Sequential execution through defined phases
Formal change control for all modifications
Baselines are established and controlled
High predictability of outcomes

details.definition: An approach where scope, time, and cost are determined early in the project lifecycle, and changes are managed through formal control processes.

example: Construction of a building where all specifications, budget, and timeline must be defined before execution. Any change requires formal approval.
exam_tips: Predictive is ideal for stable requirements and low uncertainty. Common in construction, manufacturing, and regulated industries.

title: Process Groups Overview
summary: Process Groups are logical groupings of project management activities that guide a project from initiation to closure. They are interconnected, overlapping, and iterative rather than strictly sequential.
key_concepts: Process Groups are NOT phases
They overlap and iterate throughout the project
Monitoring & Controlling is continuous
Outputs from one group feed into others

Initiating.purpose: Define and authorize the project or phase

Planning.purpose: Define the roadmap to achieve project objectives

Executing.purpose: Perform the work defined in the plan

details.interaction model: Executing and Monitoring & Controlling operate in parallel while Planning may be revisited as changes occur.

exam_tips: Process Groups are overlapping and iterative. Monitoring & Controlling occurs throughout the entire project lifecycle.

title: Knowledge Areas Overview
summary: Knowledge Areas represent specialized domains of project management expertise. Each area focuses on a specific aspect of managing a project.
key_concepts: Knowledge Areas group related processes
Each process belongs to both a Process Group and a Knowledge Area
Together they form the foundation of predictive project management
Integration Management connects all knowledge areas

knowledge_areas.name: Integration Management
knowledge_areas.purpose: Ensure all project components are properly coordinated

knowledge_areas.name: Scope Management
knowledge_areas.purpose: Define and control what is included in the project

knowledge_areas.name: Resource Management
knowledge_areas.purpose: Manage project team and physical resources

knowledge_areas.name: Governance & Control (Extended View)
knowledge_areas.purpose: Provide oversight, decision-making, and alignment with strategy

details.relationship: All knowledge areas are integrated through Integration Management and interact continuously throughout the project lifecycle.

exam_tips: Every process belongs to both a Process Group and a Knowledge Area. Integration Management is central and connects all others.

title: Process Groups × Knowledge Areas Matrix (49 Processes)
summary: This matrix maps all project management processes across Process Groups and Knowledge Areas, forming the foundation of predictive project management.
key_insights: Each process belongs to one Process Group and one Knowledge Area
Planning contains the largest number of processes
exam_tips: Understand where each process belongs. Integration processes appear across all groups and are central to project control.

title: Integration Management (Deep Dive)
summary: Integration Management ensures all project elements work together. It is the central coordination function in project management.
key_concepts: Project Manager owns integration
All knowledge areas are connected through integration
Trade-offs are managed here
Change control is centralized
examples: Balancing schedule delay vs cost increase
Deciding whether to approve a scope change
exam_tips: If the question involves coordination, trade-offs, or change control → Integration Management is the answer.

title: Project Management Plan
summary: The Project Management Plan (PMP) is the comprehensive document that describes how the project will be executed, monitored, controlled, and closed.
key_concepts: Integrated document combining all subsidiary plans
Approved before execution begins
Contains scope, schedule, and cost baselines
A living document updated through change control
Central reference for managing the project

details.definition: A formal document that integrates and consolidates all subsidiary plans and baselines to guide project execution and control.
baselines: Scope Baseline (Scope Statement + WBS + WBS Dictionary)
important distinctions: Charter defines WHAT and WHY; PMP defines HOW
PMP is detailed, while the Charter is high-level
Baselines are approved versions of plans
details.real world example: Like an operations manual that outlines processes, schedules, responsibilities, and controls required to run a complex system.

exam_tips: The Project Management Plan defines how the project will be executed. It is approved before execution and updated only through change control.

title: Project Charter
summary: The Project Charter formally authorizes the project and grants the Project Manager authority to use organizational resources.
key_concepts: Formal authorization of the project
Grants authority to the Project Manager
Created by Sponsor or PMO
High-level document
Required before planning begins

details.definition: A document issued by the project initiator or sponsor that formally authorizes the project and provides the Project Manager with authority to apply organizational resources.
who creates it: PM role: The Project Manager may assist but cannot approve the charter
important notes: The charter is created before detailed planning
Without a charter, the project should not proceed
details.real world example: Similar to an official approval letter from executive leadership that authorizes a manager to start and lead a strategic initiative.

exam_tips: The Project Charter authorizes the project and grants authority to the Project Manager. It is created by the Sponsor, not the Project Manager.

title: Scope Management
summary: Scope Management ensures that the project includes all the work required—and only the work required—to complete the project successfully.
key_concepts: Product Scope defines features and functions
Project Scope defines the work required
Scope Baseline = Scope Statement + WBS + WBS Dictionary
Scope Creep = uncontrolled scope changes
Gold Plating = adding features beyond requirements
100% Rule applies to WBS

wbs.definition: A hierarchical decomposition of the total project scope into manageable components.
rules: Lowest level is the Work Package
All work must be included in the WBS

scope issues.scope creep: Unauthorized changes to scope without formal approval
scope issues.gold plating: Adding extra features not requested by the customer

validate vs control.control scope: Monitoring and managing changes to scope baseline

exam_tips: WBS is deliverable-based, not activity-based. Validate Scope = customer acceptance. Control Scope = prevent scope creep.

title: Schedule Management
summary: Schedule Management involves defining, sequencing, estimating, and controlling project activities to ensure timely completion.
key_concepts: Activities are derived from Work Packages
Dependencies define task order
Critical Path determines project duration
Float represents scheduling flexibility
Schedule Baseline is used for performance measurement

processes.definition: Defines the core processes used to develop and control the project schedule.

dependency_types.definition: Logical relationships between project activities that determine execution sequence.
characteristics: Finish-to-Start (FS): Activity A must finish before Activity B can start (most common). Example: Foundation must be completed before building walls.
Start-to-Start (SS): Activity A must start before Activity B can start. Example: Coding starts → testing can begin early.
Finish-to-Finish (FF): Activity A must finish before Activity B can finish. Example: Documentation must complete before review ends.
Start-to-Finish (SF): Activity A must start before Activity B can finish (rare). Example: New system must start before old system is shut down.

critical_path.definition: The longest path through the project network that determines the minimum project duration.
characteristics: Activities on the critical path have zero total float
Any delay on this path delays the project
There can be multiple critical paths

float_and_slack.definition: The amount of time an activity can be delayed without impacting the project schedule.
characteristics: Total Float: time an activity can be delayed without delaying project completion
Free Float: time an activity can be delayed without delaying the next activity
Activities on critical path have zero float

leads_and_lags.definition: Adjustments applied to activity dependencies to optimize scheduling.
characteristics: Lead: allows overlap between activities (start earlier than planned dependency)
Lag: introduces delay after a dependency condition is met
Example Lead: Start testing when coding is 70% complete
Example Lag: Wait 3 days for concrete to cure before next activity

schedule_compression.definition: Techniques used to shorten project duration without reducing scope.
characteristics: Crashing – adding more resources to shorten duration (increases cost)
Fast Tracking – performing activities in parallel (increases risk)

resource_optimization.definition: Techniques used to manage resource constraints and optimize utilization.
characteristics: Resource Leveling: adjusts schedule based on resource availability (may change critical path and extend duration)
Resource Smoothing: adjusts activities within float limits without affecting critical path

exam_tips: Critical Path = longest path with zero float. Float = scheduling flexibility. Crashing increases cost, Fast Tracking increases risk. Resource Leveling may extend the schedule; Resource Smoothing does not.

title: Estimating Techniques (Predictive vs Agile)
summary: Estimating techniques are used to approximate effort, duration, or cost. Predictive approaches focus on time and cost accuracy, while Agile approaches focus on relative estimation and adaptability.
key_concepts: Different approaches use different estimation methods
Predictive focuses on accuracy and detailed planning
Agile focuses on relative effort and adaptability
Accuracy improves with more information

predictive_estimating.definition: Estimation techniques used in plan-driven projects where scope is defined upfront.
characteristics: Analogous Estimating – fast, based on historical data, low accuracy
Parametric Estimating – uses mathematical models (e.g., cost per unit)
Bottom-Up Estimating – most accurate, detailed task-level estimation
Three-Point Estimating (PERT) – reduces uncertainty using O, M, P values
Single-Point Estimating – quick best-guess estimate with higher risk
Function Point Analysis – estimates based on system functionality

agile_estimating.definition: Estimation techniques used in adaptive environments focusing on relative size and effort.
characteristics: Story Points – measure effort, complexity, and risk (not time)
T-shirt Sizing – rough size categories (XS, S, M, L, XL)
Relative Estimating – compares tasks instead of using absolute units
Affinity Estimation – groups similar work items for quick estimation

expert_and_consensus_based.definition: Estimation approaches based on expert input and team consensus.
characteristics: Wideband Delphi – multiple estimation rounds to reach consensus
Planning Poker – Agile adaptation of Delphi

multi_point_estimating.definition: Uses multiple values to account for uncertainty in estimates.

accuracy_levels.definition: Estimate accuracy improves throughout the project lifecycle.

examples: Predictive: Using historical project data to estimate duration (Analogous)
Predictive: Estimating cost per square meter (Parametric)
Agile: Using story points to estimate user stories
Agile: Using Planning Poker to reach consensus
Hybrid: Using PERT for uncertain activities
exam_tips: Predictive uses time/cost-based estimation (Bottom-Up, Analogous). Agile uses relative estimation (Story Points). PERT = (O + 4M + P) / 6. Bottom-Up = most accurate; Analogous = fastest.

title: Cost Management and Earned Value Management (EVM)
summary: Cost Management includes estimating, budgeting, and controlling project costs. Earned Value Management (EVM) integrates scope, schedule, and cost to measure project performance.
key_concepts: PV (Planned Value): budgeted work planned
EV (Earned Value): budgeted work completed
AC (Actual Cost): actual cost incurred
BAC: total approved budget
Cost and schedule performance can be measured quantitatively

interpretation.positive variance: Good (under budget or ahead of schedule)

forecasting.EAC: Estimate at Completion = BAC / CPI (most common)

insight: EVM integrates scope, schedule, and cost

exam_tips: CV = EV - AC, SV = EV - PV. CPI/SPI >1 is good. EAC = BAC / CPI is most common formula.

title: Quality Management
summary: Quality Management ensures that project deliverables meet requirements. It includes Quality Assurance (process-focused) and Quality Control (product-focused).
key_concepts: Quality = fitness for use and conformance to requirements
QA = proactive, process-oriented
QC = reactive, product-oriented
Cost of Quality includes prevention, appraisal, and failure
Quality must be planned, not inspected

QA vs QC.QC: Detects defects through inspection and testing

exam_tips: QA = prevent defects. QC = detect defects. QC produces Verified Deliverables; Validate Scope produces Accepted Deliverables.

title: Risk Management
summary: Risk Management involves identifying, analyzing, and responding to uncertainties that may impact project objectives. It includes both qualitative and quantitative assessments.
key_concepts: Risk = uncertain future event
Threats are negative risks; Opportunities are positive risks
Risk management is proactive
Qualitative = prioritization, Quantitative = numerical analysis

risk_processes.definition: Core processes used to manage project risks.

qualitative_risk_analysis.definition: Prioritizes risks based on probability and impact to determine which risks require further analysis or action.
characteristics: Classifies risks as High / Medium / Low
Focuses on ranking, not exact numbers
output: High-risk items selected for further analysis

quantitative_risk_analysis.definition: Analyzes the numerical impact of risks on project objectives such as cost and schedule.
characteristics: Uses numerical values and statistical models
formulas: Total Project Risk Exposure = sum of EMVs

risk_responses.definition: Strategies for handling risks based on type.
characteristics: Focus on reducing impact or probability

reserves.definition: Buffers included in project planning for risk handling.
characteristics: Contingency Reserve – for known risks (included in baseline)
Management Reserve – for unknown risks (not included in baseline)

examples: Qualitative: Ranking risks based on High/Medium/Low impact
Quantitative: Calculating EMV for cost risk
Using Monte Carlo simulation to forecast project completion date
Using decision tree to select best project option
exam_tips: Qualitative = prioritize risks. Quantitative = numerical analysis. EMV = Probability × Impact. Monte Carlo = simulation. Use quantitative analysis only for high-priority risks.

title: Integrated Change Control
summary: Integrated Change Control is the process of reviewing, approving, or rejecting changes to the project. It ensures that all changes are managed in a structured and controlled manner.
key_concepts: No change is implemented without formal approval
Change Control Board (CCB) reviews major changes
Baselines are updated only after approval
All approved changes must be documented
Prevents scope creep

important rules: Never implement changes based on verbal approval
All affected documents must be updated
Changes may impact scope, schedule, cost, and quality

ccb.definition: A group responsible for reviewing and approving changes

exam_tips: Never implement changes without approval. Even if a sponsor verbally agrees, formal change approval is required.

title: Procurement Management
summary: Procurement Management involves acquiring goods and services from external vendors. Choosing the right contract type is critical to managing risk.
key_concepts: Make-or-buy decisions determine sourcing strategy
Contract type defines risk allocation
Clearly defined scope improves procurement success
Formal closure of contracts is required

fixed price.description: Price is fixed; seller bears most risk

cost reimbursable.description: Buyer pays costs; buyer bears most risk

time material.description: Hybrid model; payment based on time and materials
time material.risk: Shared, but often leans toward buyer risk

exam_tips: Fixed Price = seller risk. Cost Plus = buyer risk. T&M = hybrid. Always formally close contracts.

title: Communications Management
summary: Communications Management ensures that project information is created, distributed, and understood effectively among stakeholders.
key_concepts: Project Managers spend most of their time communicating
Effective communication is critical for project success
Different stakeholders require different communication approaches
Communication must be planned and structured

communication types.push: Information is sent to recipients (e.g., emails, reports)
communication types.pull: Information is accessed by stakeholders when needed

exam_tips: Channels = n(n-1)/2. Push = send, Pull = retrieve, Interactive = two-way. Communication must be tailored to stakeholders.

title: Project Closure
summary: Project Closure is the final phase where all project work is completed, deliverables are formally accepted, and the project is officially closed.
key_concepts: Closure is a formal process, not automatic
Customer or sponsor acceptance is required
Lessons learned must be documented
Resources must be released
Project documents must be archived

closure types.successful completion: Project objectives achieved and deliverables accepted
closure types.early termination: Project stopped before completion due to business or strategic reasons

important rules: Closure must happen even if the project is terminated early
Lessons learned should be captured before team disbanding
details.phase gate: Project phases may include formal closure and review before proceeding

exam_tips: Closure sequence: Acceptance → Lessons Learned → Release Resources → Archive. Always close formally, even if terminated.

title: Organizational Process Assets (OPA) and Enterprise Environmental Factors (EEF)
summary: OPAs and EEFs are key inputs in project management. OPAs are internal assets that can be used and updated, while EEFs are environmental factors that influence the project and cannot be controlled.
key_concepts: OPAs are internal and reusable
EEFs can be internal or external but are not controllable
OPAs support execution
EEFs influence or constrain decisions

opa.definition: Processes, policies, templates, and knowledge bases within the organization

eef.definition: Conditions that influence the project but are outside the control of the project team
characteristics: Can have positive or negative impact

exam_tips: If it is a template or document → OPA. If it is a condition you cannot control → EEF.

title: Stakeholder Management
summary: Stakeholder Management involves identifying, analyzing, and engaging stakeholders to ensure their needs and expectations are addressed throughout the project.
key_concepts: Stakeholders influence project success
Must be identified early and continuously
Different stakeholders require different engagement strategies
Engagement levels must be managed actively

details.goal: Move stakeholders toward supportive or leading

exam_tips: High Power + High Interest = Manage closely. Stakeholders must be identified continuously, not only at the start.

title: Leadership Styles in Project Management
summary: Project leadership is situational. Effective Project Managers adapt their leadership style based on team maturity, project phase, and the surrounding organizational culture.
key_concepts: No single 'best' style; depends on context
Adaptability is a core leadership competency
Servant leadership is highly emphasized in modern/Agile PM
Styles range from directive to delegative
Balance between people-focus and task-focus

servant_leadership.definition: Focuses on the needs of the team members, removing obstacles, and providing resources to ensure their success.

characteristics.Shielding: Protects the team from external distractions, corporate politics, and interruptions.
characteristics.Removing_Impediments: Actively clears roadblocks, technical debts, or administrative bottlenecks.
characteristics.Empowering: Decentralizes decision-making power, giving ownership of the sprint or tasks to the team.

servant_leadership.best_for: Agile teams, self-organizing environments, and long-term project success.

transformational_leadership.definition: Inspires and motivates the team by creating a shared vision and fostering innovation.

characteristics.Visionary: Articulates a compelling, clear future state and maps out the 'Why' behind project activities.
characteristics.Intellectual_Stimulation: Challenges assumptions, takes calculated risks, and encourages creative problem-solving.
characteristics.Individual_Consideration: Acts as a mentor or coach, attending to each member's unique growth and needs.

transformational_leadership.best_for: Innovation projects, digital transformation, and navigating high ambiguity.

transactional_leadership.definition: Operates on a reward-and-punishment basis, emphasizing clear expectations, compliance, and task completion.

characteristics.Contingent_Reward: Links project objectives to specific incentives, bonuses, or professional recognition.
characteristics.Management_by_Exception: Intervenes only when performance metrics deviate from established baselines or SLAs.

transactional_leadership.best_for: Highly structured, repetitive, fixed-price, or compliance-heavy projects.

situational_leadership.definition: A flexible approach where the project manager adjusts their behavior based on the readiness and competence of team members.

characteristics.S1_Directing: High directive, low supportive; provides explicit instructions and close supervision for new members.
characteristics.S2_Coaching: High directive, high supportive; explains decisions, solicits suggestions, and supports motivation.
characteristics.S3_Supporting: Low directive, high supportive; shares decision-making authority and facilitates autonomous execution.
characteristics.S4_Delegating: Low directive, low supportive; turns over responsibility for decisions and implementation to experts.

situational_leadership.best_for: Dynamic environments with mixed team experience and changing task requirements.

laissez_faire.definition: A 'hands-off' approach where the leader provides guidance only when requested and empowers the team to work autonomously.

characteristics.Autonomous_Delegation: Gives complete freedom for team members to set goals and make operational choices.
characteristics.Passive_Oversight: Maintains minimal intervention, acting purely as a resource provider or point of escalation.

laissez_faire.best_for: Highly skilled, self-motivated, expert-level research or development teams.

power_and_influence.definition: Power is the ability to influence others in the organization.
characteristics: Referent power – based on trust and respect
Coercive power – based on authority (least effective)

examples: A Project Manager encourages the team during a tight deadline instead of pressuring them.
A leader resolves conflict by understanding both perspectives instead of imposing authority.
A PM empowers a senior team to make decisions rather than micromanaging.
exam_tips: Leadership in PMP focuses on trust, collaboration, and influence. Avoid authoritative or aggressive approaches unless absolutely necessary. Servant leadership is the preferred mindset.

title: Agile Mindset — The Foundation of All Agile Approaches
summary: Agile is not a methodology — it is a mindset. Before learning any framework (Scrum, Kanban, XP), a practitioner must internalize the values and principles that drive all agile thinking: delivering value early, embracing change, empowering people, and continuous improvement. The Agile Practice Guide (PMI, 2017) places mindset as the starting point of everything.
key_concepts: Agile Manifesto (2001): 4 values and 12 principles created by 17 software practitioners
Mindset over methodology: the values guide decisions; frameworks are just tools
Empiricism: decisions based on observation and experimentation, not prediction
Inspect and Adapt: continuously review outcomes and adjust course
Customer collaboration: ongoing partnership, not a one-time requirements handoff
Responding to change: welcome change even late in development

details.definition: Agile is a set of values and principles that guides teams toward delivering value incrementally, collaborating closely with customers, and continuously improving their process. It is defined by the Agile Manifesto and expressed through multiple frameworks and practices.

agile_manifesto_four_values.description: The Agile Manifesto states: 'We are uncovering better ways of developing software by doing it and helping others do it. Through this work we have come to value...'

values.meaning: People and communication are more important than rigid processes. A great team with a simple process outperforms a mediocre team with a sophisticated process.
Delivering functional product is more valuable than producing extensive documentation. Documentation should serve delivery, not replace it.
Ongoing partnership with the customer produces better outcomes than negotiating the contract and disappearing. The customer is a team member, not an adversary.
Adapting to new information is more valuable than rigidly following an outdated plan. Plans have value, but flexibility has more value.

agile_manifesto_four_values.critical_nuance: The Manifesto says 'while there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left MORE.' Both sides have value — Agile does not eliminate plans or documentation.

twelve_principles.description: The 12 Agile Principles elaborate on the 4 values and provide actionable guidance:
principles: Our highest priority is to satisfy the customer through early and continuous delivery of valuable software.
Welcome changing requirements, even late in development. Agile processes harness change for the customer's competitive advantage.
Deliver working software frequently, from a couple of weeks to a couple of months, with a preference for the shorter timescale.
Business people and developers must work together daily throughout the project.
Build projects around motivated individuals. Give them the environment and support they need, and trust them to get the job done.
The most efficient and effective method of conveying information to and within a development team is face-to-face conversation.
Working software is the primary measure of progress.
Agile processes promote sustainable development. The sponsors, developers, and users should be able to maintain a constant pace indefinitely.
Continuous attention to technical excellence and good design enhances agility.
Simplicity — the art of maximizing the amount of work NOT done — is essential.
The best architectures, requirements, and designs emerge from self-organizing teams.
At regular intervals, the team reflects on how to become more effective, then tunes and adjusts its behavior accordingly.

agile_vs_predictive_mindset.predictive_mindset: Plan everything upfront → execute → deliver at the end
agile_vs_predictive_mindset.agile_mindset: Plan just enough → deliver incrementally → learn and adapt continuously
agile_vs_predictive_mindset.key_shift: From 'avoiding uncertainty' to 'embracing uncertainty and learning through iteration'

when_agile_fits.description: Agile is most appropriate when the project environment has:
conditions: High uncertainty in requirements — stakeholders don't fully know what they want
Rapidly changing business environment or market conditions
Need for early delivery of value before full completion
Complex problems where the solution is not yet known
High stakeholder engagement and availability for frequent feedback

agile_suitability_factors.description: PMI Agile Practice Guide describes four dimensions to assess agile suitability:

dimensions.agile_friendly: Open to change, values experimentation, trust-based, collaborative
Complex, innovative, changing requirements, benefits from early delivery
Available, engaged, willing to participate in reviews, tolerant of change

details.real_world_example: A startup building a new mobile app has no fully-defined requirements — they know the general direction but expect user feedback to shape the product. They release an MVP in 6 weeks, gather data, and iteratively improve. This is classic agile thinking: deliver early, learn from reality, adapt. If they had spent 18 months writing a full specification and building it without feedback, they would likely build the wrong product.

outputs: Shared agile mindset across team and stakeholders
exam_tips: The Agile Manifesto has 4 values (left over right) and 12 principles. 'Responding to change over following a plan' — plans still have value; agile values flexibility MORE. Agile is a mindset first, framework second. If the exam asks 'what drives agile decisions' → values and principles, not any specific framework.

title: Scrum Framework — Roles, Events, and Artifacts
summary: Scrum is the most widely used agile framework. It is a lightweight framework within which teams can employ various processes and techniques to generate value. The Scrum Guide (2020) defines three accountabilities, five events, and three artifacts — all governed by the empirical pillars of Transparency, Inspection, and Adaptation.
key_concepts: Three accountabilities: Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers
Five events: Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, Sprint Retrospective
Three artifacts: Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment
Three commitments: Product Goal, Sprint Goal, Definition of Done
Empirical pillars: Transparency, Inspection, Adaptation
Time-box: every event has a maximum duration — cannot be extended

transparency.definition: All significant aspects of the work must be visible to those responsible for the outcome
examples: Sprint progress visible via burndown chart

inspection.definition: Scrum users frequently inspect Scrum artifacts and progress toward agreed goals
examples: Daily Scrum inspects progress toward Sprint Goal

adaptation.definition: If any aspect deviates outside acceptable limits, adjustments must be made as soon as possible
examples: Product Backlog refined after Sprint Review

product_owner.primary_responsibility: Maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team
key_activities: Developing and explicitly communicating the Product Goal
Creating and clearly communicating Product Backlog items
Ensuring the Product Backlog is transparent, visible, and understood
product_owner.authority: Product Owner is the SOLE decision-maker on product priorities — the team must respect their decisions
product_owner.one_person: The Product Owner is one person, not a committee. A committee may exist behind them, but the PO represents their decisions.
product_owner.real_world_example: The PO for an e-commerce app decides: 'This sprint we focus on checkout optimization — not the wishlist feature — because checkout abandonment is costing us $200K/month.' The team trusts this priority without needing further justification.

scrum_master.primary_responsibility: Establishing Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide and helping everyone understand Scrum theory and practice
serves_the_scrum_team: Coaching team members in self-management and cross-functionality
Helping the team focus on creating high-value Increments that meet the Definition of Done
Removing impediments to the team's progress
Ensuring all Scrum events take place and are positive and productive
serves_the_product_owner: Helping find techniques for effective Product Goal definition and Product Backlog management
Helping the team understand the need for clear and concise Product Backlog items
Facilitating stakeholder collaboration as requested or needed
serves_the_organization: Leading, training, and coaching the organization in Scrum adoption
Helping employees and stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach for complex work
scrum_master.servant_leader: The Scrum Master is a servant leader — their power comes from serving and enabling others, not from authority or task assignment
scrum_master.NOT_a_pm: The Scrum Master does NOT assign tasks, manage performance, or own the project budget. These are common misconceptions.

developers.primary_responsibility: Creating any aspect of a usable Increment each Sprint
accountabilities: Creating a plan for the Sprint — the Sprint Backlog
Instilling quality by adhering to a Definition of Done
Adapting their plan each day toward the Sprint Goal
Holding each other accountable as professionals
developers.self_organizing: Developers decide HOW to accomplish the work — no one tells them how to turn backlog items into Increments
developers.cross_functional: Together, the Developers have all the skills necessary to create value each Sprint — no external dependencies for core work

sprint.definition: The heartbeat of Scrum — a fixed-length event of one month or less in which all other events occur
sprint.time_box: Maximum 1 calendar month (most teams use 1-2 weeks)
characteristics: No changes that endanger the Sprint Goal are made
Product Backlog is refined as needed
Scope may be clarified and renegotiated with PO as more is learned
sprint.sprint_goal: A single objective for the Sprint that provides coherence and focus — created during Sprint Planning, committed to by Developers
sprint.cancelling_sprint: ONLY the Product Owner can cancel a Sprint — only if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete. This is rare and should be avoided.

sprint_planning.definition: Initiates the Sprint by laying out the work to be performed
sprint_planning.time_box: Maximum 8 hours for a one-month Sprint (shorter for shorter Sprints)

three_topics.output: Sprint Goal — the PO proposes, the whole Scrum Team collaborates to finalize

three_topics.topic: What can be Done this Sprint?
three_topics.output: Selected Product Backlog items — Developers forecast what they can complete

three_topics.topic: How will the chosen work get done?
three_topics.output: Sprint Backlog — Developers decompose selected items into tasks of 1 day or less

sprint_planning.input_requirement: Only items that meet the Definition of Ready should be brought into Sprint Planning

daily_scrum.definition: A 15-minute event for the Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog
daily_scrum.time_box: 15 minutes, same time and place daily
daily_scrum.purpose: Inspect and adapt — not a status report to the Scrum Master or anyone else
daily_scrum.participants: Developers only (Scrum Master and PO attend as observers unless they are also Developers)
three_classic_questions: What did I do yesterday that helped the team meet the Sprint Goal?
What will I do today to help the team meet the Sprint Goal?
Do I see any impediment that prevents me or the team from meeting the Sprint Goal?
daily_scrum.important_note: The 3 questions are a common technique but NOT required by the Scrum Guide. The team can use any structure as long as the goal is inspection and adaptation.
daily_scrum.common_mistake: Running Daily Scrum as a status meeting for managers. It is owned by and for the Developers.

sprint_review.definition: Scrum Team and stakeholders inspect the outcome of the Sprint and determine future adaptations
sprint_review.time_box: Maximum 4 hours for a one-month Sprint
sprint_review.purpose: Inspect the PRODUCT Increment and adapt the Product Backlog
activities: Team presents the Increment and demonstrates it to stakeholders
Product Owner reviews Product Backlog in light of new information
Discussion of what to do next (informs Sprint Planning)
sprint_review.NOT_a_demo: Sprint Review is more than a demo — it is an inspect-and-adapt conversation about the entire product direction
sprint_review.output: Revised Product Backlog reflecting new insights and priorities

sprint_retrospective.definition: The Scrum Team inspects how the last Sprint went with regard to individuals, interactions, processes, tools, and Definition of Done
sprint_retrospective.time_box: Maximum 3 hours for a one-month Sprint
sprint_retrospective.purpose: Inspect the PROCESS and create a plan for improvements
three_questions: What went well during the Sprint?
How can we commit to improving in the next Sprint?
sprint_retrospective.output: Identified improvements to implement in the NEXT Sprint — most impactful improvement added to Sprint Backlog
sprint_retrospective.distinction_from_sprint_review: Sprint Review = inspect the PRODUCT. Sprint Retrospective = inspect the PROCESS.

product_backlog.definition: An emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product — the single source of work for the Scrum Team
characteristics: Owned and managed exclusively by the Product Owner
Never complete — evolves as product and environment evolve
Items higher in the list are more refined (clearer, smaller, more estimated)
Refined continuously through Product Backlog Refinement
product_backlog.commitment: Product Goal — the long-term objective for the Scrum Team; every Sprint brings the product closer to the Product Goal
product_backlog.backlog_refinement: Ongoing activity (not a formal event) of breaking down and adding detail to Product Backlog items — typically consumes no more than 10% of Developers' capacity per Sprint

sprint_backlog.definition: Composed of: the Sprint Goal (why), the set of Product Backlog items selected for the Sprint (what), and a plan for delivering the Increment (how)
sprint_backlog.ownership: Owned and managed by the Developers — not by the Scrum Master or Product Owner
sprint_backlog.commitment: Sprint Goal — provides flexibility in terms of exact work while maintaining coherence of purpose
sprint_backlog.dynamic: Updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned — Developers add, remove, and refine tasks daily

increment.definition: A concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal — each Increment is additive to all prior Increments and thoroughly verified
increment.must_be_usable: An Increment must be potentially releasable at the end of every Sprint — whether or not the PO chooses to release it
increment.multiple_per_sprint: Multiple Increments may be created within a Sprint — work does not need to wait for Sprint end to be released
increment.commitment: Definition of Done — a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required

definition_of_done.definition: A formal description of the quality standards an Increment must meet to be considered complete
definition_of_done.purpose: Creates transparency, shared understanding, and consistency across the team
characteristics: Created by the Scrum Team if not defined by the organization
Applies to ALL items — not negotiable per story
May evolve over time (teams typically make DoD stricter as they improve)
definition_of_done.example: Code reviewed, unit tests passing, integration tests passing, security scan clean, documentation updated, deployed to staging environment
definition_of_done.vs_acceptance_criteria: Acceptance Criteria = story-specific conditions set by PO. DoD = team-wide quality standard applied to every item.

inputs: Stakeholder feedback from previous Sprint Review
exam_tips: Only the PO can cancel a Sprint. Scrum Master is a servant leader — does NOT assign tasks. Sprint Review = inspect PRODUCT (stakeholders attend). Sprint Retrospective = inspect PROCESS (Scrum Team only). DoD applies to ALL items — not negotiable. Sprint Backlog is owned by Developers. Product Backlog is owned by Product Owner.

title: Kanban — Visualizing Flow and Managing Work-in-Progress
summary: Kanban is a flow-based agile approach that focuses on visualizing work, limiting work-in-progress (WIP), and continuously improving throughput. Unlike Scrum, Kanban has no fixed iterations, no prescribed roles, and no mandatory ceremonies — work is pulled continuously based on capacity. The Agile Practice Guide (PMI) describes Kanban as one of the key agile approaches alongside Scrum.
key_concepts: Visualize the workflow: make all work and its status visible on a board
Limit WIP: cap the number of items in any given stage to expose bottlenecks
Manage flow: optimize the movement of work through the system
Make policies explicit: everyone understands the rules governing work
Implement feedback loops: regular reviews of flow metrics
Improve collaboratively: use models and scientific thinking to evolve the system
Lead time vs cycle time: two critical flow metrics

details.definition: Kanban is a method for managing knowledge work with an emphasis on just-in-time delivery while not overloading team members. Work items are visualized on a Kanban board to give participants a view of progress and process from start to finish.

kanban_board.structure: A visual representation of the workflow with columns representing stages
kanban_board.wip_limits: Each column (except Backlog and Done) has a maximum number of items allowed at once
kanban_board.swim_lanes: Optional horizontal rows to separate different types of work or different teams

six_core_practices.description: Map every step of the workflow and make all work items visible on the board
six_core_practices.benefit: Creates shared understanding of how work actually flows — exposes hidden work and bottlenecks

six_core_practices.description: Set maximum number of items allowed in each workflow stage
six_core_practices.benefit: Prevents overloading, exposes bottlenecks, encourages 'stop starting, start finishing'
six_core_practices.example: In Progress column WIP limit = 3: when 3 items are in progress, no new item can be pulled until one moves forward

six_core_practices.description: Monitor and report on the flow of work through the system
six_core_practices.goal: Smooth, predictable, fast flow — eliminate wait time and batch processing

six_core_practices.description: Document and display the rules governing work: definition of ready, definition of done, WIP limits, escalation criteria
six_core_practices.benefit: Reduces ambiguity; everyone makes decisions using the same rules

six_core_practices.description: Hold regular meetings to review flow metrics and process health
Use the scientific method (hypothesis → experiment → measure → learn) to evolve the system
six_core_practices.approach: Make changes incrementally rather than radical overhauls

lead_time.definition: Total time from when a work item is requested to when it is delivered
lead_time.formula: Lead Time = time item enters the backlog → time item is completed
lead_time.customer_perspective: What the customer experiences — how long to get what they asked for
lead_time.example: Customer submits feature request on Monday; it is delivered the following Wednesday = 9 business days lead time

cycle_time.definition: Time from when work actively BEGINS on an item to when it is completed
cycle_time.formula: Cycle Time = time work starts on item → time item is completed
cycle_time.team_perspective: What the team controls — how long work takes once started
cycle_time.example: Developer picks up the story on Thursday; it is done by Friday = 2 days cycle time
cycle_time.relationship: Lead Time = Cycle Time + Wait Time. Large gap between them = too much waiting.

throughput.definition: Number of work items completed per unit time
throughput.use: Forecasting — 'at this throughput, when will the backlog be done?'
throughput.example: Team completes 12 stories per week → 60-story backlog will take ~5 weeks

cumulative_flow_diagram.definition: Area chart showing the count of items in each workflow stage over time
what_to_look_for: Band widening = items accumulating in that stage (bottleneck)
Flat lines = work has stopped flowing
Consistent parallel bands = healthy, predictable flow

comparison.Kanban: No prescribed roles — existing titles/roles are maintained

comparison.Scrum: Sprint Planning at start of each Sprint
comparison.Kanban: Continuous — pull work when capacity is available
No sprint-level commitment — work flows continuously

comparison.Scrum: Sprint Goal protected within Sprint; changes wait for next Sprint
comparison.Kanban: Changes can be introduced anytime if capacity allows

comparison.Scrum: Development teams with iterative product work

details.real_world_example: A software support team handles bug reports continuously. There is no natural 'end of sprint' — bugs arrive daily and must be resolved quickly. They use Kanban: new bugs enter 'Incoming', analysts triage them to 'Prioritized', engineers pull from 'Prioritized' to 'In Progress' (WIP limit = 2 per engineer), then move to 'In Review' and 'Done'. The WIP limit prevents engineers from juggling 5 bugs at once — they finish one before starting the next. Average cycle time drops from 8 days to 3 days.

inputs: Flow metrics (lead time, cycle time, throughput)
exam_tips: Kanban has NO fixed sprints, NO required roles, NO mandatory ceremonies. Lead time = customer experience (request to delivery). Cycle time = team experience (start to done). WIP limit exceeded → stop pulling new work; finish existing items first. CFD band widening = bottleneck. Kanban excels in support, operations, and maintenance contexts.

title: Extreme Programming (XP) — Technical Excellence in Agile
summary: Extreme Programming (XP) is an agile framework focused on technical practices that enable teams to deliver high-quality software rapidly and sustainably. Created by Kent Beck in the late 1990s, XP 'turns up the dial' on good software engineering practices — taking proven techniques and applying them more intensively. The PMI Agile Practice Guide references XP as a key agile framework.
key_concepts: Five values: Communication, Simplicity, Feedback, Courage, Respect
Technical practices are first-class citizens alongside people practices
Test-Driven Development (TDD): write tests before writing code
Pair Programming: two developers, one keyboard — continuous code review
Continuous Integration (CI): integrate and test code multiple times per day
Refactoring: continuously improve the design of existing code
Simple Design: do the simplest thing that could possibly work — no gold plating

details.definition: XP is a disciplined approach to software development that values simplicity, communication, feedback, and courage. It prescribes a set of core engineering practices that, when combined, dramatically improve software quality and team responsiveness to change.

five_values.description: Team members must communicate openly and frequently — with each other and with customers. XP prefers face-to-face conversation and practices like pair programming that force continuous communication.
Do the simplest thing that could possibly work. Avoid building things you might need in the future — YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It). Simple code is easier to understand, test, and change.
Get feedback as fast as possible at all levels: test results (seconds), pair programming feedback (minutes), customer feedback (days/weeks). The faster the feedback loop, the cheaper the correction.
Have the courage to tell the truth about estimates, to refactor code that works, to delete code that is no longer needed, to try new approaches. XP teams don't hide problems.
Team members must respect each other and the customer. Everyone's contributions are valued. No one is allowed to break the build and just leave.

planning.description: Collaborative planning between developers and customers to determine the scope of the next release. Customer defines value; developers define cost (effort). Together they set priorities.
Release working software in small, frequent increments. Minimizes risk, enables feedback, and provides early business value.
A simple, shared story of how the whole system works — a common vocabulary that all stakeholders understand.

designing.description: Design only for current requirements. Pass all tests, express every intention clearly, eliminate duplication, use the fewest possible elements.
Continuously restructure existing code to improve its design without changing its external behavior. 'Don't live with broken windows.'

coding.description: Write a failing test first, write the minimum code to pass it, then refactor. Cycle: Red (fail) → Green (pass) → Refactor.
coding.benefit: Ensures 100% test coverage, forces clear thinking about requirements before coding, reduces debugging time

coding.description: Two developers work together at one computer: the 'driver' writes code, the 'navigator' reviews and thinks strategically. Roles rotate frequently.
benefits: Continuous code review — defects caught immediately
Knowledge sharing — no single points of failure
Higher code quality than solo development (research-backed)
Mentoring opportunity for less experienced developers
coding.misconception: Pair programming is NOT less productive — it is 15% slower in raw output but produces 15% fewer defects, which more than compensates in reduced rework

coding.description: Any developer can change any code anywhere in the codebase at any time. No 'my code' — only 'our code'. Prevents knowledge silos.
All code looks as if it was written by a single person — agreed-upon standards that make collective ownership possible.
Developers integrate their code into a shared repository multiple times per day. Each integration triggers an automated build and test suite.
coding.benefit: Integration problems are found and fixed within hours, not after weeks of divergent development

testing.description: Customers write acceptance tests that define when a story is done. These tests are automated and run continuously.

environment.description: Work no more than 40 hours per week. Teams that work overtime produce less — they accumulate fatigue, make more mistakes, and burn out. XP treats this as an engineering constraint, not just a welfare concern.
A real customer (or customer proxy) is available to the team full-time. They answer questions immediately, clarify requirements, and make priority decisions in real-time.
The team works in a large, open room — easy conversation, overhearing important discussions, shared awareness of project state.

xp_vs_scrum.scrum: Framework for managing iterative delivery — focuses on roles, events, and artifacts. Silent on specific engineering practices.
xp_vs_scrum.xp: Engineering discipline — prescribes specific technical practices (TDD, pair programming, CI). Can be used INSIDE Scrum sprints.
xp_vs_scrum.combined: Many high-performing teams use Scrum for structure and XP practices for engineering excellence — this combination is highly effective.

details.real_world_example: A team writing financial calculation software uses TDD: before implementing any formula, a developer writes a test that fails (e.g., 'IRR calculation for this cash flow should return 12.3%'). They then write the minimum code to pass the test, then refactor for clarity. Result: 847 automated tests that run in 2 minutes, giving the team confidence to refactor aggressively. When a regulatory change requires formula updates, they make the change, run the tests, and deploy in 4 hours — not 4 weeks.

exam_tips: XP = technical excellence practices. TDD = write test FIRST (Red → Green → Refactor). Pair Programming produces FEWER defects despite slightly slower output. Sustainable pace = 40 hours/week maximum. XP and Scrum are complementary: Scrum for structure, XP for engineering quality. On-site customer is an XP practice — immediate feedback, not periodic reviews.

title: Agile Planning — From Vision to Iteration
summary: Agile planning is multi-layered and continuous — not a one-time upfront event. The PMI Agile Practice Guide describes planning across multiple horizons: vision, roadmap, release, iteration, and daily. Each level provides increasing detail for a shorter time horizon. Agile teams plan just enough to act, then continuously refine as they learn.
key_concepts: Progressive elaboration: plan in detail only what you are about to execute
Rolling wave planning: future work stays high-level; near-term work is detailed
Multiple planning horizons: Vision → Roadmap → Release → Iteration → Daily
Just-in-time (JIT) planning: detail emerges when needed, not upfront
Cone of uncertainty: estimates improve as the project progresses
Story mapping: visualizing the product's user journey to organize the backlog

planning_onion.description: The Agile Practice Guide uses the 'planning onion' — concentric layers from strategic to daily — to show that planning operates at multiple levels simultaneously

layers.detail: Why does this product exist? What problem does it solve?
layers.example: 'We will be the leading B2B expense management platform in Southeast Asia by 2027'

layers.detail: High-level feature themes and milestones — WHAT and roughly WHEN
layers.example: Q1: Core expense submission; Q2: Approval workflow; Q3: Analytics dashboard

layers.detail: Which features/stories will be in the next release? At current velocity, when?
layers.example: Release 1.0 in 10 sprints: 25 stories, velocity 8 points/sprint = ~200 points capacity

layers.detail: Exactly which stories will be completed this sprint, decomposed into tasks
What am I doing today to contribute to the Sprint Goal?
layers.example: 'Today I will complete the API integration for the expense upload feature'

product_backlog_refinement.definition: The ongoing process of adding detail, estimates, and order to Product Backlog items — preparing them for future Sprints
product_backlog_refinement.timing: Continuous — not a single event. Typically 10% or less of Developers' capacity per Sprint.
activities: Breaking large items (Epics) into smaller stories
Ordering items by priority and value
product_backlog_refinement.definition_of_ready: Items at the top of the backlog should meet the Definition of Ready before being brought into Sprint Planning

invest_criteria.description: Good user stories meet the INVEST criteria:
criteria: Independent: can be developed and delivered without depending on other stories
Negotiable: details can be negotiated between PO and Developers
Valuable: delivers clear benefit to users or business
Estimable: team can estimate the effort required
Testable: has clear acceptance criteria that can be verified

user_story_format.template: As a [type of user], I want [some goal] so that [some reason/benefit]

examples.story: As an expense submitter, I want to upload receipts from my phone so that I don't have to keep physical copies
acceptance_criteria: Given I am logged in on mobile, when I click 'Add Receipt', I can select an image from my camera roll
File formats supported: JPG, PNG, PDF up to 10MB

three_Cs.Card: The written story — brief, fits on a card
three_Cs.Conversation: The discussion that fleshes out details between PO, team, and users
three_Cs.Confirmation: The acceptance criteria that confirm the story is done

story_points.definition: Relative unit of measure that captures the effort, complexity, and uncertainty of a user story
story_points.relative_not_absolute: A 4-point story is twice as complex as a 2-point story — not necessarily twice as many hours
story_points.fibonacci_scale: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21 — gaps increase as size increases, reflecting growing uncertainty
story_points.benefit: Avoids false precision of hour estimates; enables faster estimation through relative comparison

planning_poker.definition: A consensus-based estimation technique using numbered cards
process: PO reads a user story
Each Developer privately selects a card representing their estimate
All reveal simultaneously
Outliers (highest and lowest) explain their reasoning
Discussion until consensus is reached
Re-estimate if needed
planning_poker.benefit: Prevents anchoring bias (first person to speak influences others), surfaces hidden complexity, builds shared understanding

affinity_estimating.definition: Rapid estimation technique for large backlogs — silently group stories by relative size
affinity_estimating.process: Team places stories in columns (XS, S, M, L, XL) silently, then discuss disagreements
affinity_estimating.use_when: Estimating 20+ stories quickly at the start of a release plan

velocity.definition: Average story points completed per Sprint over the last 3-5 Sprints
velocity.use: Forecasting — estimate how many Sprints to complete remaining backlog
velocity.example: If average velocity = 32 points and backlog has 256 points → approximately 8 Sprints remaining
velocity.important: Velocity is a TEAM metric (not individual), a HISTORICAL average (not a commitment), and should not be used to compare teams

release_planning.definition: Determining what features will be delivered in an upcoming release and when
process: PO prioritizes the Product Backlog by value
Team estimates stories (if not already done)
Calculate velocity (average of last 3-5 Sprints)
Count stories that fit within capacity: Sprints × Velocity = total points
Identify which stories fit → release scope
Determine release date based on Sprint count
release_planning.flexibility: In agile, release plan is a FORECAST, not a contract. If velocity changes or priorities shift, the release plan updates.

fixed_date_vs_fixed_scope.fixed_date: Release happens on set date — team delivers maximum value possible by then (scope is flexible)
fixed_date_vs_fixed_scope.fixed_scope: Release includes specific features — date moves based on velocity (date is flexible)
fixed_date_vs_fixed_scope.recommendation: Choose one: fix the date OR fix the scope. Fixing both is a trap.

exam_tips: Agile planning is multi-level: Vision → Roadmap → Release → Iteration → Daily. Story points are RELATIVE (not hours). Velocity = average completed points per sprint (last 3-5). 'Fixed date OR fixed scope' — not both. Definition of Ready = criteria for bringing a story into a Sprint. Planning Poker prevents anchoring bias.

title: Agile Teams — Self-Organization, Cross-Functionality, and High Performance
summary: Agile teams are structured differently from traditional project teams. The PMI Agile Practice Guide emphasizes that high-performing agile teams are small, cross-functional, self-organizing, and co-located (or effectively virtual). These characteristics — not any specific framework — are what enable agility. The team is the fundamental unit of agile delivery.
key_concepts: Self-organizing: team decides HOW to accomplish the work — no external direction needed
Cross-functional: team has ALL skills needed to deliver value each iteration
Small team size: 5-9 members (Amazon's two-pizza rule)
T-shaped skills: breadth across disciplines + depth in one specialty
Team stability: same people across multiple Sprints builds trust and velocity
Psychological safety: team members feel safe to take risks and speak up
Servant leadership: leaders enable rather than direct

self_organization.definition: The team determines how to best accomplish their work given the goals set by the Product Owner — no external manager assigns tasks or dictates approach
what_it_means_in_practice: During Sprint Planning, Developers collectively decide who works on what
During Daily Scrum, Developers coordinate among themselves — no manager assigns daily tasks
If a Developer is stuck, they ask a teammate — not a manager
The team can change their technical approach without external approval
what_it_does_NOT_mean: Anarchy — the team still has a Product Owner setting direction and a Scrum Master ensuring process
No accountability — the team is collectively accountable for Sprint deliverables
Ignoring organizational constraints — teams operate within organizational policies
benefits: Faster decisions — no waiting for management approval on daily work
Higher ownership — people who choose their work are more committed to it
Better solutions — people closest to the problem design the solution
More learning — team develops skills through autonomy

cross_functionality.definition: The team collectively has ALL skills necessary to deliver a potentially shippable increment every Sprint — without depending on people outside the team
what_cross_functional_means: No hand-offs to separate QA team at end of Sprint — testing happens within the Sprint
No waiting for DBA team to design the schema — a team member can do it
No waiting for UX team approval — a team member has UX skills (or the PO fills that gap)

t_shaped_skills.definition: Team members have broad knowledge across multiple disciplines (the horizontal bar) plus deep expertise in one area (the vertical bar)
t_shaped_skills.example: A developer with deep Java expertise also understands testing, can write SQL, and knows basic UX principles — enabling flexible task allocation
t_shaped_skills.benefit: Reduces bottlenecks — if the specialist is unavailable, others can contribute

generalist_vs_specialist.challenge: Pure specialists create bottlenecks; pure generalists lack depth
generalist_vs_specialist.solution: T-shaped or I-shaped people on the team — broad enough to collaborate, deep enough to specialize

optimal_team_size.too_small: Less than 3: insufficient skills, one absence cripples the team
optimal_team_size.too_large: More than 9: communication complexity explodes (n(n-1)/2 channels), coordination costs rise, self-organization becomes difficult
optimal_team_size.scaling: When more people are needed, create multiple teams (each 5-9) working on the same product — this is where scaling frameworks (SAFe, LeSS) come in

team_dynamics_tuckman.model: Tuckman's Team Development Stages apply to agile teams

stages.characteristics: Team meets, polite, figuring out roles and norms
stages.velocity: Low — team is learning to work together
stages.pm_action: Facilitate team norms / working agreement creation, clarify goals

stages.characteristics: Conflict emerges — about technical approach, priorities, working style
stages.pm_action: Coach through conflict, reinforce psychological safety, facilitate retrospectives
stages.important: Storming is NORMAL and necessary — suppressing it leads to worse outcomes

stages.characteristics: Team develops shared norms, processes, and trust

stages.pm_action: Delegate fully, protect from interference, focus on removing systemic impediments

stages.characteristics: Project ending, team members transitioning away
stages.velocity: May decline as members mentally check out
stages.pm_action: Celebrate success, facilitate knowledge transfer, acknowledge individual contributions

psychological_safety.definition: The belief that one will not be punished or humiliated for speaking up with ideas, questions, concerns, or mistakes
why_it_matters: Teams with high psychological safety surface problems early — when they are cheap to fix
Teams without it hide problems — which compound until they cause crises
Innovation requires risk — people only take risks when they feel safe
how_to_build_it: Leader models vulnerability: 'I don't know — let's figure it out together'
Thank people who raise problems: 'Good catch — that would have been expensive'
Never visibly react negatively to bad news — the team is watching
Conduct blameless post-mortems: 'What did the system allow? How do we fix the system?'
Create explicit space for dissent: 'Who sees this differently?'

working_agreements.definition: Explicit team norms created collaboratively about how the team will work together
examples: Core hours: 10am-4pm — everyone available for collaboration
Response time to Slack messages: within 2 hours during core hours
Definition of Done: reviewed by peer, tests passing, deployed to staging
Meeting norms: start on time, camera on, phones away
Conflict resolution: raise in retrospective or directly with person involved
working_agreements.process: Created by the team (not management), revisited in retrospectives, evolved as the team matures

servant_leadership.definition: Leaders who prioritize serving the team's needs over exercising authority
behaviors: Shield the team from organizational noise and interruptions
Ask 'What do you need?' not 'Why isn't this done?'
Develop team members' skills and careers

leadership_vs_management.traditional_management: Plan, organize, control — tell people what to do and measure compliance
leadership_vs_management.agile_leadership: Create conditions for the team to succeed — set direction, remove obstacles, trust the team
leadership_vs_management.practical_implication: An agile leader does not assign daily tasks, does not review every decision, does not require status meetings — they trust and enable

exam_tips: Self-organizing = team decides HOW (not what or when — PO decides what). Cross-functional = ALL skills within the team (no external dependencies per iteration). Optimal size 5-9. Storming is NORMAL — coach through it, don't suppress it. Servant leadership: serve the team to enable performance. Psychological safety is a prerequisite for effective Agile teams.

title: Agile Metrics — Measuring Progress and Performance
summary: Agile teams measure progress through working software and flow-based metrics — not documentation or activity. The PMI Agile Practice Guide identifies several key metrics: velocity, burndown/burnup charts, cumulative flow diagrams, lead time, and cycle time. These metrics answer the team's most important questions: Are we delivering value? Are we on track? Where are our bottlenecks?
key_concepts: Working software is the PRIMARY measure of progress (Agile Manifesto Principle 7)
Velocity: average story points completed per Sprint — used for forecasting
Burndown Chart: remaining work decreasing over time
Burnup Chart: completed work increasing over time (also shows scope changes)
Cycle time and lead time: flow efficiency metrics from Kanban
Escaped defects: quality metric — bugs found after delivery
Metrics should inform decisions, not be used for individual performance evaluation

velocity.definition: The average number of story points a team completes per Sprint, calculated over the last 3-5 Sprints
velocity.formula: Velocity = Sum of completed story points in a Sprint (items must meet Definition of Done)
velocity.how_to_calculate_stable_velocity: Average of last 3-5 Sprints. Discard outliers (holidays, team changes).

use_for_forecasting.example: Team velocity = 34 points/Sprint. Product Backlog has 204 estimated points remaining. Forecast: 204 / 34 = 6 Sprints to complete.
use_for_forecasting.range: Always present as a range: at low velocity (28) = 7-8 Sprints; at high (40) = 5 Sprints. Honest forecasting is a range, not a single number.

what_velocity_is_NOT: NOT a commitment (it is a historical average)
NOT a performance target (pushing for higher velocity degrades quality)
NOT comparable across teams (different story point scales and contexts)
NOT meaningful for individuals (velocity is a TEAM metric)

velocity_trends.stable: Healthy team in Performing stage — predictable delivery
velocity_trends.increasing: Team improving, better estimation, reducing technical debt
velocity_trends.decreasing: Signal of systemic problems: technical debt accumulation, morale issues, unresolved impediments, team changes
velocity_trends.wildly_variable: Inconsistent estimating, team instability, or frequent scope changes

burndown_chart.definition: A line chart showing remaining work (Y-axis) vs time (X-axis), trending toward zero

sprint_burndown.ideal_line: Straight diagonal from starting points on Day 1 to zero on Day 10
what_to_look_for: Flat periods: team is blocked or work is not being completed
Steep drops: large items completed; may indicate poor task granularity
Line above ideal: behind schedule — unlikely to meet Sprint Goal
Line below ideal: ahead of schedule — may pull in additional items
