release_burndown.y_axis: Remaining story points in Product Backlog
release_burndown.challenge: If scope is added, the burndown may go UP — making it look like the team is moving backward even when they're delivering

burndown_chart.limitation: Burndown does not show scope changes — if backlog grows, the line doesn't accurately reflect team productivity

burnup_chart.definition: A chart showing COMPLETED work (Y-axis) increasing toward a scope line over time
burnup_chart.advantage_over_burndown: Shows BOTH completed work AND total scope — scope changes are visible as the scope line moving up
components: Total Scope Line: current total story points in backlog (moves up when scope is added)
Completed Work Line: cumulative story points done (moves up each Sprint)
Gap: the remaining work — when lines meet, release is complete
burnup_chart.when_to_use: Prefer burnup when scope is frequently changing — it shows the full picture honestly

sprint_goal_achievement.definition: Did the team achieve the Sprint Goal? Binary yes/no per Sprint
sprint_goal_achievement.importance: More meaningful than velocity — a team can deliver high velocity but miss the Sprint Goal if they cherry-pick easy stories

escaped_defects.definition: Number of bugs discovered AFTER delivery to users (post-release)
escaped_defects.formula: Escaped Defect Rate = Bugs found in production / Total bugs found
escaped_defects.target: As close to zero as possible — every escaped defect represents a quality process failure

team_satisfaction.definition: Subjective measure of team morale and engagement
team_satisfaction.why_it_matters: Sustained high performance requires sustained team health

cycle_time_distribution.definition: A scatter plot of cycle times for completed items, with percentile lines
cycle_time_distribution.use: Set Service Level Expectations: '85% of standard requests complete within 5 days'
cycle_time_distribution.outliers: Items far above the 85th percentile need investigation — why did they take so long?

throughput.definition: Number of items completed per unit time (week, Sprint)
throughput.forecast_use: If throughput = 12 items/week and backlog has 96 items → ~8 weeks to complete
throughput.advantage_over_velocity: Doesn't require story point estimation — count of items is sufficient

metrics_anti_patterns.problem: Teams use different story point scales, different definitions of complexity, and different team sizes — comparison is meaningless and destructive
Teams respond by inflating estimates (story point inflation) — velocity appears to increase while actual productivity doesn't
Destroys team collaboration — developers optimize for their own stories rather than helping teammates
Hides problems until they become crises — psychological safety requires honest metric sharing

details.real_world_example: A team's Sprint burndown is flat for the first 5 days of a 10-day Sprint. At Day 5, they have completed 0 of 32 story points. The Scrum Master asks in the Daily Scrum: 'It seems like nothing is moving through to Done — what's blocking us?' The team reveals they've all been working on tasks independently but none have met the Definition of Done because testing requires a shared environment that's been broken for 5 days. The Scrum Master immediately escalates to fix the test environment. By Day 10, they deliver 24 points. The burndown made the systemic problem visible — without it, the issue might have surfaced only at Sprint Review.

exam_tips: Velocity = average completed story points (NOT a commitment, NOT comparable across teams). Burndown → remaining work. Burnup → completed work + scope line (better when scope changes). Sprint Goal achievement is more meaningful than velocity alone. Flat burndown = blocked work. Never use velocity to compare teams or evaluate individuals.

title: Scaled Agile — Coordinating Multiple Agile Teams
summary: When a single Scrum team is not enough — when the product is too large, the organization too complex, or multiple teams must coordinate — scaling frameworks provide structures for maintaining agility at scale. The PMI Agile Practice Guide identifies SAFe, LeSS, Disciplined Agile (DA), and Spotify model as key scaling approaches. Each has different tradeoffs.
key_concepts: Scaling challenge: Agile works naturally for 5-9 people; coordination costs rise steeply above this
SAFe (Scaled Agile Framework): most widely adopted; Agile Release Trains (ARTs) of 50-125 people
LeSS (Large Scale Scrum): one Scrum, many teams; minimal additional roles and ceremonies
Disciplined Agile (DA): toolkit approach — choose what fits your context
PI Planning: SAFe's centerpiece event for multi-team coordination
Communities of Practice (CoP): cross-team knowledge sharing

why_scaling_is_hard.problem: A single agile team of 7 has 21 communication channels. Three teams of 7 have 21 within each team PLUS inter-team coordination channels. Dependencies, integration points, and conflicting priorities multiply rapidly.
scaling_challenges: Shared components require coordination (database, API, infrastructure)
Consistent Definition of Done across teams
Portfolio-level prioritization when teams compete for limited resources
Maintaining agile mindset as organizational bureaucracy increases

levels.team_level: Individual Scrum/Kanban teams deliver features in 2-week Sprints
levels.program_level: Agile Release Train (ART) — 5-12 teams aligned around a common solution, delivering a Program Increment (PI) every 8-12 weeks
levels.large_solution_level: Multiple ARTs coordinate on very large systems
levels.portfolio_level: Strategy and investment decisions; aligns ARTs with business strategy

key_roles.description: Scrum Master for the ART — facilitates PI Planning, removes impediments at program level, coaches ART on SAFe practices
Owns the Program Backlog and Program Increment content — equivalent of Product Owner at the ART level
Provides architectural guidance and governance for the entire ART
Key stakeholder responsible for business outcomes — attends PI Planning and Sprint Reviews

PI_planning.definition: All-hands event (typically 2 days) where all teams in the ART plan their next Program Increment together
PI_planning.attendees: All team members, Product Managers, RTE, Business Owners, Architects, stakeholders
outcomes: PI Objectives for each team (committed and uncomitted)

ROAM.R: Resolved — risk is resolved during PI Planning
ROAM.O: Owned — someone owns it and will manage it
ROAM.A: Accepted — risk is accepted as is

PI_planning.why_important: PI Planning is the primary mechanism for cross-team alignment — it replaces months of email chains and coordination meetings with 2 days of face-to-face planning

program_increment.definition: A time-boxed interval (8-12 weeks) in which an ART delivers incremental value through a series of Sprints
program_increment.typical_structure: 4 development Sprints + 1 Innovation and Planning (IP) Sprint
program_increment.ip_sprint_purpose: Time for innovation, technical debt reduction, PI Planning prep, and testing at system level

LeSS.philosophy: Apply Scrum to multiple teams with minimal additional rules and roles — 'More with LeSS'

LeSS_basic.structure: One Product Backlog, one Product Owner, one Sprint, one Sprint Review — but multiple teams
LeSS_basic.key_addition: Overall Retrospective — all teams + PO + Scrum Masters meet to coordinate process improvements

LeSS_huge.addition: Area Product Owners for different product areas; Requirement Areas

LeSS.vs_SAFe: LeSS adds far fewer roles and ceremonies than SAFe — more faithful to original Scrum principles. SAFe is more prescriptive and enterprise-friendly. Neither is universally better.

disciplined_agile.philosophy: A toolkit, not a prescriptive framework — teams choose the practices that fit their context
disciplined_agile.key_concept: Context counts — what works for a 5-person startup is different from what works for a 500-person enterprise
disciplined_agile.guided_continuous_improvement: DA provides decision frameworks to help teams choose the right approach for their specific situation

communities_of_practice.definition: Voluntary groups of practitioners from different teams who share a common interest in a specific domain and meet regularly to learn and share
examples: Agile CoP: Scrum Masters from all teams meet weekly to share practices
DevOps CoP: engineers across teams share CI/CD learnings
Frontend CoP: UI developers discuss standards and new technologies
communities_of_practice.benefit: Spreads knowledge and standards horizontally across teams without creating bureaucratic governance
communities_of_practice.vs_formal_roles: CoPs are informal and voluntary — they work through influence and shared learning, not authority

details.real_world_example: A bank is building a new digital platform. Five product teams each handle a domain: Accounts, Payments, Loans, Cards, and Analytics. They are all on one Agile Release Train. Every 10 weeks, all 45 people attend PI Planning — 2 days in a large room. By the end, each team has objectives for the next 10 weeks, the program board shows 23 cross-team dependencies (each with an owner), and 8 risks have been ROAMed. The RTE tracks the program board weekly. Teams deliver in 2-week Sprints and demo at a combined System Demo every Sprint. This is SAFe in practice.

methods_tools: Inspect and Adapt workshop (end of PI)
exam_tips: SAFe: ARTs of 50-125 people, PI Planning every 8-12 weeks, RTE = Scrum Master for ART. LeSS: minimal additions to Scrum (one PO, one backlog, multiple teams). Disciplined Agile (DA) is owned by PMI — it is a toolkit, not a framework. PI Planning = 2-day event where all ART teams plan together. ROAM = Resolved, Owned, Accepted, Mitigated.

title: Hybrid Approaches — Combining Predictive and Agile
summary: Most real-world projects are neither purely agile nor purely predictive — they are hybrid. The PMI Agile Practice Guide dedicates a section to hybrid approaches, recognizing that different parts of a project may benefit from different methodologies. Effective hybrid requires deliberate design — not accidental mixing of approaches.
key_concepts: Hybrid = deliberate combination of predictive and adaptive methods
Neither pure waterfall nor pure agile — tailored to the specific context
Different workstreams can use different approaches within the same project
The project manager's role is to design the right blend
Tailoring: PMI's principle of adapting methodology to fit the project
Agile for uncertainty; predictive for stability and compliance

common_drivers: Regulated environment requires documentation (predictive) but development is complex (agile)
Hardware component is fixed-design (predictive); software component is iterative (agile)
Customer contract is fixed-price (predictive constraints); team works in Sprints internally (agile)
Legacy system integration requires predictive planning; new features are developed agilely
Organization is transitioning from waterfall to agile — hybrid is the intermediate state

iterative_waterfall.description: Waterfall phases overall, but iterative development within the execution phase
iterative_waterfall.example: Requirements phase → Iterative development Sprints → Testing phase → Deployment
iterative_waterfall.use_when: Customer requires fixed-price contract and milestone-based payments but benefits from iterative development

agile_with_predictive_governance.description: Agile development teams operate in Sprints, but governed by predictive reporting, CCB, and stage gates
agile_with_predictive_governance.example: Scrum teams within SAP implementation — Sprints for configuration work, but change management and go/no-go gates are predictive
agile_with_predictive_governance.use_when: Large enterprise with strong governance requirements but development complexity benefits from agile

waterfall_phases_agile_execution.description: Initiation and planning are predictive (charter, business case, high-level plan); execution is agile (Sprints delivering features)
waterfall_phases_agile_execution.example: Project Charter → High-level roadmap → Agile Sprint delivery → Predictive project closure
waterfall_phases_agile_execution.use_when: Organization requires predictive planning artifacts but benefits from iterative delivery

mixed_workstreams.description: Different streams use different approaches — integrated at the project level
mixed_workstreams.example: Data center infrastructure (predictive waterfall) + mobile app development (Scrum) + compliance documentation (Kanban) — all coordinated by one PM with a unified roadmap
mixed_workstreams.challenge: Synchronizing release milestones between streams with different cadences

questions: What is the team's agile capability?

steps.step: 2. Select the approach for each workstream
steps.guidance: Stable, compliant, well-understood → Predictive. Uncertain, complex, innovation-heavy → Agile.
How will agile Sprint outputs connect to predictive milestones? Use Roadmap as the bridging artifact.
Define which agile artifacts satisfy which predictive governance requirements (e.g., Sprint backlog = WBS equivalent for reporting)
Report predictive metrics (EVM) at the program level; use agile metrics (velocity, burndown) at team level

common_hybrid_artifacts.role: Bridges predictive milestones and agile release plans — visible to all workstreams
WBS at the deliverable level; Sprints within WBS deliverables
Predictive tool used across all workstreams — risks identified in agile Retrospectives feed into the program-level register
Shows Sprint milestones alongside predictive deliverable dates

hybrid_pitfalls.description: Calling something 'sprints' but still requiring complete upfront design and no changes — this is waterfall with agile theater
hybrid_pitfalls.symptom: Team follows Sprints but PO is not available, changes are not welcomed, DoD doesn't include working software

hybrid_pitfalls.description: Using Scrum without appropriate documentation for a regulated environment
hybrid_pitfalls.symptom: Audit finds no traceability between requirements and deliverables

hybrid_pitfalls.description: Agile software team and predictive infrastructure team work independently and only integrate at the end
hybrid_pitfalls.symptom: Integration failures at go-live that could have been caught earlier

tailoring_principle.definition: PMI's principle that project managers should deliberately adapt their approach to fit the specific project, team, and organizational context — rather than applying a single methodology rigidly
tailoring_principle.pmbok_7_emphasis: PMBOK 7th Edition makes tailoring explicit — no one approach fits all projects
how_to_tailor: Assess project complexity, uncertainty, and stakeholder needs
Determine which practices add value in this context
Remove or modify practices that create overhead without value
Continuously revisit the approach in retrospectives

details.real_world_example: A pharmaceutical company is developing a new patient portal. The FDA regulatory submission requires comprehensive documentation and traceability (predictive). The actual software development is complex with evolving UX requirements (agile). Solution: Predictive planning phase → Scrum development Sprints (2 weeks) → Formal validation phase (predictive). Sprint Reviews serve as UAT sessions. Sprint Backlog items are traced to regulatory requirements in a traceability matrix. The PM maintains an integrated program roadmap used in governance meetings.

outputs: Sprint outputs connected to milestone deliverables
exam_tips: Hybrid = deliberate combination, not accidental mixing. Different workstreams can use different approaches. Roadmap is the primary bridging artifact. Tailoring is a PMI principle (PMBOK 7): adapt the approach to the context. Common exam scenario: regulatory environment + complex development → hybrid. Sprint outputs can satisfy predictive governance requirements if properly documented.

title: Agile in the Organization — Adoption, Change, and Culture
summary: Adopting agile is an organizational change initiative — not just a process change for development teams. The PMI Agile Practice Guide emphasizes that agile adoption fails not from lack of technical knowledge but from organizational culture, leadership behavior, and structural barriers. Successful agile organizations develop an agile culture, agile-supportive leadership, and a learning organization.
key_concepts: Agile adoption is an organizational change, not just a team process change
Organizational agility: the ability of the whole organization to respond to market changes
Leadership must model agile behavior — not just mandate it
Impediments to agile often come from organizational systems (HR, finance, governance)
Psychological safety is an organizational prerequisite for agile
Agile Center of Excellence (CoE) or PMO supports enterprise agile adoption

technical_challenges: Teams trained in agile theory but lacking coaching support
Legacy systems that resist iterative development
organizational_challenges: HR systems that reward individual performance over team outcomes
Annual budgeting cycles that conflict with agile's incremental funding needs
Governance frameworks requiring extensive upfront documentation
Middle management feeling threatened by self-organizing teams
Stakeholders unwilling to commit time for Sprint Reviews and backlog refinement
cultural_challenges: Fear of failure in a blame culture
Hierarchy that punishes teams for surfacing bad news
Resistance to transparency — agile makes problems visible
Short-term thinking vs agile's sustainable pace philosophy

traditional_vs_agile.traditional: Functional silos → hand-offs between departments → slow delivery
traditional_vs_agile.agile_friendly: Cross-functional teams aligned around products or value streams → fast delivery

product_vs_project.project_model: Fund projects (temporary teams, defined scope) → disband team when done
product_vs_project.product_model: Fund products (stable teams, evolving backlog) → team persists as long as product exists
product_vs_project.agile_preference: Product model — stable teams build knowledge and velocity; project model resets this with every new project

value_stream_alignment.definition: Organizing teams around the flow of value delivery from concept to customer — end-to-end
value_stream_alignment.example: Instead of separate Dev, QA, and Ops departments that hand off to each other, one team owns the full flow from code to production

enabling_behaviors: Protect the team from interruptions and context-switching
Trust the team to self-organize — resist micromanagement
Make decisions transparently and explain the 'why'
Model learning: be open about mistakes and lessons learned
Remove systemic impediments (process, policy, tool) the team cannot remove
Attend and engage genuinely in Sprint Reviews
Respect team capacity — don't add ad-hoc requests mid-Sprint
undermining_behaviors: Bypassing the Product Owner to give the team direct requirements
Requesting detailed time tracking per task (implies distrust)
Comparing team velocities to pressure lower-performing teams
Using retrospective findings as performance evidence against individuals

agile_pmo.traditional_pmo_role: Enforce methodology compliance, track project status, manage project portfolio
agile_pmo.agile_pmo_role: Enable and coach teams, remove organizational impediments, provide governance frameworks that work with agile, share best practices
agile_pmo.evolution: PMOs that cannot evolve from compliance to enablement become obstacles to agile adoption
supportive_pmo_activities: Develop agile-compatible reporting (burnup charts alongside EVM)
Aggregate portfolio-level metrics without dictating team-level velocity

agile_maturity.level_1_ad_hoc: Teams experiment with agile practices inconsistently
agile_maturity.level_2_managed: Team-level agile is working; leaders support it but don't practice it
agile_maturity.level_3_defined: Agile practices standardized across teams; leadership models agile values
agile_maturity.level_4_quantitatively_managed: Flow metrics and quality data drive continuous improvement
agile_maturity.level_5_optimizing: Organizational agility — the whole company responds to market changes; agile is the culture, not just a practice

common_anti_patterns_in_adoption.description: Management mandates 'we are now agile' without supporting the change — teams relabel activities but nothing changes
common_anti_patterns_in_adoption.fix: Leadership must change behavior first; team change follows

common_anti_patterns_in_adoption.description: We use Scrum, BUT we don't do retrospectives. BUT the Product Owner isn't available. BUT we can't say no to mid-sprint changes.
common_anti_patterns_in_adoption.fix: Identify what the 'BUT' is protecting — usually an organizational constraint that must be addressed directly

common_anti_patterns_in_adoption.anti_pattern: Agile for delivery, waterfall for planning
common_anti_patterns_in_adoption.description: Teams develop in Sprints, but the roadmap is locked for 18 months and cannot change
common_anti_patterns_in_adoption.fix: Decoupling delivery cadence from planning horizon — agile delivery requires agile planning

common_anti_patterns_in_adoption.description: Adopting Scrum ceremonies without XP technical practices — results in 'agile with no engineering quality'
common_anti_patterns_in_adoption.fix: Invest in test automation, CI/CD, and clean code practices as enablers of sustainable agility

details.real_world_example: A 3,000-person insurance company decides to 'go agile.' They train 200 teams in Scrum. Six months later: teams are doing Sprints but Product Owners attend 30% of Sprint Reviews, HR still measures individual output, finance still requires annual project funding (not product funding), and managers still assign tasks in Stand-up. Velocity is low and teams are frustrated. The problem is not the teams — it is the system around them. True transformation requires HR, Finance, IT Governance, and Leadership to change simultaneously.

inputs: Market and competitive pressure for agility
methods_tools: ADKAR Change Model (Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement)
exam_tips: Agile adoption is an ORGANIZATIONAL change, not just a team methodology change. Failures often come from organizational systems (HR, finance, governance) not from team-level implementation. ScrumBut = using Scrum but removing the parts that are uncomfortable — usually signals organizational resistance. PMO must evolve from compliance to enablement. Leaders must MODEL agile behavior, not just mandate it.

title: Agile Requirements — User Stories, Epics, and the Product Backlog
summary: In agile, requirements are not specified comprehensively upfront — they emerge through collaboration and are expressed progressively in the form of user stories, epics, and themes. The Product Backlog is the living requirements document, continuously refined. This approach reduces waste (building the wrong thing) and embraces the reality that requirements evolve.
key_concepts: User Story: short description of a feature from the user's perspective — Card, Conversation, Confirmation
Epic: large user story that must be broken into smaller stories before it can be completed in a Sprint
Theme: collection of related user stories or epics that form a coherent business objective
Acceptance Criteria: specific conditions that must be met for a story to be accepted
Definition of Ready: conditions a story must meet before entering a Sprint
Product Backlog: ordered, living list of all work — the single source of truth for product requirements

requirements_in_agile_vs_predictive.predictive: All requirements are defined, documented, baselined, and change-controlled before development begins
requirements_in_agile_vs_predictive.agile: Requirements are defined incrementally — high-level early, detailed just before development. The backlog is the requirements document.
why_agile_approach_works: Customers often don't know what they want until they see something working
Early detailed requirements are often wrong — based on assumptions that change
JIT (Just-in-Time) requirements reduce rework from changed requirements
Working software provides better feedback than written specifications

user_stories_in_depth.format: As a [type of user], I want [goal] so that [reason/benefit]

three_Cs.Card: Written story — brief, fits on a 3x5 index card. Intentionally brief to prevent over-specification.
three_Cs.Conversation: The real requirements are in the conversations between the team, PO, and users — the card is just a placeholder for these discussions.
three_Cs.Confirmation: Acceptance criteria — the tests that confirm the story is complete and correct.

good_story_examples: As a frequent traveler, I want to receive push notifications when my flight status changes so that I can adjust my plans proactively.
As an expense approver, I want to see all pending approvals in one dashboard so that I can process them efficiently without navigating multiple screens.
bad_story_examples: As a system, I should store user preferences. (Technical story — no user value visible)
As an admin, I want the system to be fast. (Not specific — 'fast' is unmeasurable and untestable)

INVEST_criteria.Independent: Can be developed without depending on another incomplete story
INVEST_criteria.Negotiable: Details negotiable between PO and team; not a rigid contract
INVEST_criteria.Valuable: Delivers real benefit to users or business — 'so that' clause must be genuine
INVEST_criteria.Estimable: Team can estimate effort — if not, too vague or too big
INVEST_criteria.Small: Can be completed within one Sprint
INVEST_criteria.Testable: Has concrete acceptance criteria that can be verified

story_hierarchy.theme: Strategic objective or business capability (e.g., 'Improve customer self-service')
story_hierarchy.epic: Large feature or capability, spanning multiple Sprints (e.g., 'Customer account management portal')
story_hierarchy.story: Deliverable feature in one Sprint (e.g., 'Customer can reset their own password')
story_hierarchy.task: Technical work item, usually within a Sprint (e.g., 'Implement password strength validation')

splitting_stories.definition: Breaking large stories or epics into smaller, independently deliverable stories
splitting_stories.why: Stories must be small enough to complete in one Sprint with working software

techniques.example: Purchase order story → Create PO / Submit PO / Approve PO / Receive items
Discount calculation → Standard discount / Loyalty discount / Promotional discount
Payment processing → Credit card / PayPal / Bank transfer — each as separate stories
Basic search (text match) in Sprint 1 → Advanced search (filters, sorting) in Sprint 3

acceptance_criteria_in_depth.definition: Specific, testable conditions that a deliverable must satisfy for it to be accepted by the Product Owner

given_when_then.format: Given [initial context], When [action occurs], Then [expected outcome]
given_when_then.example: Given I am a registered user, When I enter my email and click 'Reset Password', Then I receive a reset email within 60 seconds

formats.checklist: Simple bullet list of conditions: ✓ Password must be 8+ characters, ✓ Must contain at least one number, ✓ Confirmation email sent

characteristics_of_good_AC: Testable: can be verified by a tester without ambiguity
Specific: clear enough that two people reading it reach the same conclusion
Focused: tests the story's behavior, not technical implementation
Written BEFORE development begins — not after

ordering_vs_prioritizing.distinction: Agile teams 'order' the backlog (PO decides relative positioning of EVERY item), not just 'prioritize top 10'
ordering_vs_prioritizing.practical_impact: Every item has a unique position — no ties. This forces hard trade-off decisions.

backlog_prioritization_techniques.description: Must have / Should have / Could have / Won't have this time
backlog_prioritization_techniques.use_when: Initial release planning, communicating scope to stakeholders

backlog_prioritization_techniques.description: 2x2 grid: High Value + Low Effort = do first; Low Value + High Effort = consider dropping
backlog_prioritization_techniques.use_when: Prioritizing a new batch of features

backlog_prioritization_techniques.description: SAFe technique: prioritize by (Business Value + Time Criticality + Risk Reduction) / Job Duration
backlog_prioritization_techniques.use_when: Large program backlog prioritization in SAFe context

backlog_prioritization_techniques.description: Categorizes features by customer delight: Basic (expected), Performance (more = better), Delighters (unexpected wow)

story_mapping.definition: A visual technique (Jeff Patton) that organizes user stories across two dimensions: user activities (horizontal) and story detail level (vertical)

structure.backbone: High-level user activities across the top (the user's journey from left to right)
structure.walking_skeleton: Minimum viable stories for each activity — the thinnest path through the map
structure.detail: More detailed stories below — options, edge cases, enhancements

story_mapping.benefit: Makes the 'whole product' visible at a glance, enables release planning by drawing horizontal lines through the map
story_mapping.real_world_example: For a hotel booking app: backbone = [Search] → [Select room] → [Book] → [Manage booking] → [Check-in] → [Check-out]. Walking skeleton = one story per column (basic search, select room type, enter credit card, view booking, mobile check-in, receipt). Everything below the skeleton is a future enhancement.

methods_tools: User Story format (As a / I want / So that)
exam_tips: User story format: As a [user] / I want [goal] / So that [benefit]. INVEST = Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable. Acceptance criteria written BEFORE development. Epic = too large for one Sprint, must be split. Product Backlog is ORDERED (not just prioritized) — PO decides position of every item. Story Map backbone = user journey left-to-right.

title: Agile Quality — Building Quality In from the Start
summary: In agile, quality is not inspected in at the end — it is built into every Sprint through practices like TDD, continuous integration, peer review, and a rigorous Definition of Done. The PMI Agile Practice Guide emphasizes that technical quality practices are not optional extras — they are what makes sustainable agility possible. Without quality practices, teams accumulate technical debt that slows them to a halt.
key_concepts: Built-in quality: defects are prevented, not just detected
Definition of Done (DoD): quality gate applied to every increment
Test-Driven Development (TDD): tests written before code — ensures coverage
Continuous Integration (CI): code integrated and tested multiple times per day
Refactoring: improving code design without changing behavior
Technical debt: future cost of shortcuts taken now
Retrospective: regular process for improving team quality practices

agile_quality_philosophy.traditional_view: Build first → Test afterward → Fix defects → Release
agile_quality_philosophy.agile_view: Build quality in from the start → Continuous testing → Prevent defects → Release confidently

cost_of_fixing_defects.during_development: Cheapest — developer finds and fixes immediately
cost_of_fixing_defects.post_release: Expensive — customer found it; includes support cost, reputation damage, emergency fix

definition_of_done_quality_gate.purpose: Ensures every increment meets a consistent quality bar — preventing 'almost done' items from accumulating as undone technical debt
sample_robust_dod: Code reviewed by at least one peer
Unit tests written and passing (>80% code coverage)
Acceptance criteria verified and signed off by PO
No new critical or high severity bugs introduced
Security scan completed with no new high findings
Deployed to staging environment and smoke-tested
definition_of_done_quality_gate.evolving_dod: Teams typically start with a simple DoD and strengthen it over time as their test automation and CI/CD maturity grows
definition_of_done_quality_gate.non_negotiable: DoD applies to ALL items — the team cannot declare a story done without meeting DoD, even under deadline pressure

technical_debt.definition: The implied future cost of additional rework caused by choosing an expedient solution now instead of a better approach

types.description: Consciously taking a shortcut to meet a deadline — with the intent to pay it back
types.example: Hardcoding a configuration value to make the deadline, with a ticket to fix it next Sprint

types.description: Unintentional — poor design decisions made without awareness of the better approach
types.example: Copy-pasting code instead of refactoring — didn't know better

types.description: Small shortcuts that compound over time into a significant burden
types.symptom: Velocity declining over Sprints despite team stability and same Story complexity

managing_technical_debt: Allocate a percentage of each Sprint (e.g., 20%) to debt reduction
Make debt visible on the backlog — PO can prioritize it alongside features
Don't let debt accumulate silently — surface it in retrospectives
Track debt indicators: cycle time, defect rate, deployment frequency

continuous_integration.definition: Developers merge their code changes into a shared repository multiple times per day; each merge triggers an automated build and test suite
benefits: Integration problems found within hours (not after weeks of divergence)
Always-passing build gives confidence to refactor
practices: Merge at least once per day

continuous_delivery.definition: Every code change that passes automated tests is automatically deployed to a staging environment — ready to release to production with one click
continuous_delivery.benefit: Reduces risk of large, infrequent deployments — small deployments are easier to roll back

continuous_deployment.definition: Every code change that passes automated tests is automatically deployed to PRODUCTION — no human decision
continuous_deployment.example: Amazon reportedly deploys to production every 11 seconds
continuous_deployment.requirement: Extremely high automated test coverage and monitoring

agile_testing_quadrants.description: Framework for thinking about different types of tests and when they are needed

quadrants.purpose: Verify code works correctly — fast feedback during development

quadrants.tests: Functional tests, story acceptance tests, prototype testing (automated + manual)
quadrants.purpose: Verify the right thing is being built

quadrants.tests: Exploratory testing, user acceptance testing, usability testing (manual)
quadrants.purpose: Find what the automated tests miss; verify user experience

shift_left_testing.definition: Moving testing earlier in the development lifecycle — ideally, tests are written BEFORE code (TDD)
shift_left_testing.benefit: Cheaper defect detection; forces clear thinking about requirements before implementation
shift_left_testing.contrast: Traditional waterfall: test at the end → expensive, high-stakes, lots of defects

details.real_world_example: A fintech startup has a strict Definition of Done: every story must have unit tests (>85% coverage), pass security scan, be reviewed by a peer, and be deployed to staging. In Sprint 7, a developer finishes a payment feature 2 days before Sprint end but the security scan reveals a SQL injection vulnerability. The story is NOT marked Done. The developer fixes the vulnerability, reruns the scan, and it passes on Day 9. This is Definition of Done working correctly — the 'done' story that ships is genuinely done, and the team can trust their staging environment.

inputs: Team quality standards and coding guidelines
exam_tips: Agile quality = built in, not inspected in. DoD is NON-NEGOTIABLE — a story cannot be Done without meeting it. Technical debt = future rework cost of shortcuts. CI = integrate and test multiple times/day. Shift-left = test earlier in development (TDD takes it to the extreme: test FIRST). Accumulated technical debt causes velocity decline over time — visible on velocity chart.

title: Business Analysis — Overview, Role, and Value
summary: Business Analysis (BA) is the set of tasks and techniques used to work as a liaison between stakeholders in order to understand the structure, policies, and operations of an organization, and to recommend solutions that enable the organization to achieve its goals. The PMI Guide to Business Analysis positions BA as a critical bridge between business problems and effective solutions — preventing the most costly error in project management: building the right solution to the wrong problem.
key_concepts: Business Analysis: identifying business needs and recommending solutions that deliver value
Business Analyst (BA): practitioner who performs BA tasks — may be a dedicated role or performed by PM, PO, or SME
Needs Assessment: the starting point — understand the problem before proposing solutions
Requirements: conditions or capabilities needed to solve a problem or achieve an objective
Stakeholders: anyone who has an interest in the outcome — internal and external
Solution: a specific outcome that addresses a business problem or opportunity
Value: the net benefit realized — financial and non-financial

details.definition: According to the PMI Guide to Business Analysis, business analysis is the application of knowledge, skills, tools, and techniques to determine problems and opportunities, identify business needs, and recommend viable solutions for meeting those needs and for delivering value to stakeholders.

why_BA_matters.the_problem: The Standish Group Chaos Report consistently shows that a leading cause of project failure is poor requirements — building the wrong thing, building too much, or building without understanding the real need.
statistics: ~39% of projects succeed (on time, budget, scope)
Poor requirements account for a significant portion of failures
Cost of fixing a requirement error in production can be 100x the cost of finding it in requirements phase
BA_prevents: Solving the wrong problem (symptom vs root cause confusion)
Scope creep from poorly defined boundaries

dedicated_BA_role.description: A separate practitioner focused entirely on requirements and business analysis
dedicated_BA_role.common_in: Large enterprises, complex system implementations, regulated industries

pm_performing_BA.description: Project Manager performing BA activities in addition to project management
pm_performing_BA.common_in: Small projects, organizations without dedicated BAs
pm_performing_BA.risk: Conflict of interest — PM may rush requirements to begin execution

product_owner_as_BA.description: In Agile contexts, the Product Owner performs many BA activities

sme_as_BA.description: Subject Matter Experts contributing their domain knowledge to requirements
sme_as_BA.limitation: SMEs know the domain but may not know BA techniques — facilitation by a skilled BA improves outcomes

BA_knowledge_areas_pmi_guide.description: The PMI Guide to Business Analysis organizes BA work into the following knowledge areas:

areas.focus: Identify and define the business problem or opportunity before proposing solutions
Identify, analyze, and engage stakeholders throughout the BA process
Draw out requirements from stakeholders using various techniques
Examine, model, and validate requirements to ensure completeness and correctness
Track requirements through the lifecycle; manage changes
Assess whether the delivered solution actually solves the problem

predictive.timing: Requirements are elicited and documented comprehensively upfront — before development begins
predictive.challenge: Requirements written too early are often wrong or incomplete — expensive to change later

agile.timing: Requirements are elicited just-in-time, progressively elaborated as the team learns
agile.advantage: Requirements evolve with customer learning — reduces risk of building the wrong thing
agile.BA_role: Product Owner or embedded BA refines backlog continuously

hybrid.approach: High-level requirements upfront (themes, epics) + detailed requirements just-in-time per iteration

details.real_world_example: A hospital wants to 'improve patient flow.' Without BA, the IT team builds a new scheduling system (a solution). With BA: the analyst conducts interviews, observes workflows, and discovers the real problem is that discharge paperwork takes 4 hours — not scheduling. The right solution is a document automation tool — 10x cheaper and 10x more effective than the scheduling system. This is the value of needs assessment before solution design.

exam_tips: BA is about identifying the RIGHT problem before proposing solutions. In Agile, the Product Owner performs many BA activities. Poor requirements are a leading cause of project failure. BA bridges business stakeholders and technical teams. Key distinction: the BA understands WHAT is needed; the developer decides HOW to build it.

title: Needs Assessment — Defining the Real Business Problem
summary: Needs Assessment is the first and most critical phase of business analysis — it ensures the project is solving the right problem. The PMI Guide to Business Analysis defines it as the process of identifying the problem or opportunity, determining root causes, understanding stakeholder needs, and assessing the current and desired states before any solution is proposed. Skipping Needs Assessment is the primary source of wasted project investment.
key_concepts: Problem statement: clear articulation of the gap between current and desired state
Root cause analysis: finding the real cause of the problem (not just symptoms)
Current state ('As-Is'): how things work today
Future state ('To-Be'): how things should work after the solution
Gap analysis: the delta between current and future state = the work to be done
Business need: the underlying organizational necessity driving the project
Feasibility analysis: assessing whether a solution is viable before committing

details.definition: Needs Assessment is the process of identifying a problem or opportunity, analyzing it to understand root causes and contributing factors, assessing the current state, defining the desired future state, and identifying the gap between them — all before proposing solutions.

needs_assessment_steps.description: Understand what triggered this initiative — a pain point, a regulatory change, a market opportunity, or a strategic direction
questions: What is happening that should not be happening?
What is not happening that should be?
What is the business impact of the current situation?
needs_assessment_steps.pitfall: Accepting the problem as stated without questioning it — stakeholders often present solutions as problems

needs_assessment_steps.description: Document how the business currently operates — processes, systems, people, data, rules
needs_assessment_steps.output: Current state description — processes, pain points, metrics, root causes

needs_assessment_steps.description: Drill beneath symptoms to find the actual cause — addressing only symptoms guarantees recurrence

example.symptom: Customer complaints about slow order processing
5_whys: Why slow? → Orders require manual data entry
Why manual? → The new CRM doesn't integrate with the order system
Why no integration? → IT budget was cut mid-project
Why was budget cut? → The business case didn't quantify integration ROI
Root cause: Incomplete business case led to under-funded integration

needs_assessment_steps.description: Describe the desired outcome — what success looks like after the solution is implemented
needs_assessment_steps.example: Order processing time reduced from 48 hours to under 4 hours. Customer satisfaction score improves from 65% to 85% within 6 months of implementation.

needs_assessment_steps.description: Identify the difference between current state and desired state — this gap defines the scope of required change
needs_assessment_steps.output: Gap analysis table: Current Capability vs Required Capability vs Gap vs Recommended Change
needs_assessment_steps.example_gap: Current: Manual entry into 3 separate systems. Desired: Single data entry with automatic propagation. Gap: Need integration middleware + updated business process.

needs_assessment_steps.description: Evaluate potential solution options before recommending one

feasibility_dimensions.question: Can the organization actually operate this solution? Do people have the skills?
Can this be built with available technology? What are the technical risks?
Does the expected benefit justify the cost? Positive NPV? Acceptable payback period?
Can the solution be delivered within the required timeframe?
Does the solution comply with all applicable laws and regulations?

problem_vs_solution_confusion.common_mistake: Stakeholders often state solutions as problems — the BA must dig beneath to find the real need

examples.real_need: 'We need to improve customer retention by tracking all touchpoints consistently'
examples.BA_response: Investigate whether a new CRM is the right solution, or whether the current system configured properly would suffice

examples.stated: 'We need to hire 10 more customer service agents'
examples.real_need: 'We need to reduce average handle time so existing agents can service more customers'
examples.BA_response: Process analysis revealed 60% of calls were about order status — a self-service portal reduced call volume by 40%, eliminating the need for more agents

business_case_support.definition: The BA supports business case development by quantifying the problem, sizing the opportunity, and providing analysis that justifies the investment
BA_contributions: Quantified problem statement (cost of the problem per year)
Multiple solution options with cost/benefit estimates
business_case_support.BA_does_not: Make the go/no-go decision — that is the Sponsor/steering committee based on BA's analysis

details.real_world_example: An insurance company wants to build a mobile app for claims submission. Before any development, the BA conducts 30 customer interviews and analyzes 6 months of claims data. Findings: 78% of customers submit claims via phone, with 45-minute average call time. The #1 complaint is 'I don't know the status of my claim.' Root cause: no self-service status tracking exists. The BA recommends: (1) SMS status notifications — 4 weeks, $30K. (2) Web portal — 12 weeks, $200K. (3) Native mobile app — 24 weeks, $800K. The business case analysis shows option 1 addresses 80% of complaints at 4% of the cost of option 3. The BA's analysis saves the company $770K.

inputs: Financial data (current cost of the problem)
exam_tips: Needs Assessment comes BEFORE solution design. Root cause analysis prevents solving symptoms. Gap Analysis = As-Is vs To-Be = project scope. Feasibility has 5 dimensions: Operational, Technical, Financial, Time, Legal. The BA recommends solutions but does NOT make the investment decision — that belongs to the Sponsor.

title: Stakeholder Engagement in Business Analysis
summary: Effective stakeholder engagement is the foundation of successful business analysis. The PMI Guide to Business Analysis identifies stakeholder identification, analysis, and engagement as ongoing BA activities — not a one-time exercise. BAs must identify ALL relevant stakeholders (including those who might resist), understand their perspectives, build trust, and facilitate productive collaboration. Requirements that lack broad stakeholder input will inevitably be incomplete or conflicted.
key_concepts: Stakeholder: anyone with an interest in or impact on the project outcome
Business stakeholders vs technical stakeholders: different perspectives, different needs
Power/Interest Grid: tool for prioritizing stakeholder engagement strategy
Stakeholder analysis: understanding influence, interest, and attitude
Internal vs external stakeholders
Champion vs resistor: identify and work with both
HiPPO (Highest Paid Person's Opinion): anti-pattern where authority overrides evidence

stakeholder_identification.definition: Systematically discovering all individuals, groups, and organizations who may affect or be affected by the project
stakeholder_identification.when: Begin at project initiation; continue throughout — new stakeholders emerge as the project progresses

internal_stakeholders: Project Sponsor — funds and authorizes the project
Business Owner — owns the process being changed
Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) — deep domain knowledge
End Users — will use the resulting solution daily
IT team — will build and maintain the solution
Operations team — will support the solution
Legal and Compliance — ensure regulatory adherence
Finance — budget holders and financial impact assessors
external_stakeholders: Customers and clients — end recipients of the product/service
Regulatory bodies — must approve or certify the solution
Vendors and suppliers — provide components or services
Community groups — affected by organizational change

hidden_stakeholders.definition: Stakeholders not immediately obvious who can significantly impact or be impacted by the solution
examples: A department whose workflow changes as a downstream result
A union representative whose members' job descriptions change
An audit team who will review the new system for compliance
hidden_stakeholders.finding_them: Ask known stakeholders: 'Who else might be affected by this? Who else should be part of this conversation?'

power_interest_grid.definition: 2x2 matrix plotting stakeholders by their power (ability to influence) and interest (level of concern)

quadrants.engagement: Frequent, detailed collaboration; involve in decisions; review requirements with them
quadrants.example: Business Owner whose department the system will transform

quadrants.engagement: Regular high-level updates; seek their input on major decisions; don't overwhelm with details
quadrants.example: CFO who approves budget but won't use the system

quadrants.engagement: Regular updates; listen to their feedback; they often surface important insights
quadrants.example: End users whose workflow will change significantly

quadrants.engagement: Periodic check-ins; notify of significant changes
quadrants.example: Adjacent department minimally affected by the change

attitude_assessment.description: Beyond power and interest, assess each stakeholder's attitude toward the change

categories.description: Actively promotes and advocates for the project
categories.strategy: Leverage them to influence others; involve them in stakeholder engagement

categories.description: Positive about the change but not actively promoting it
categories.strategy: Keep engaged; provide information they need to advocate if asked

categories.description: Neither supports nor opposes — waiting to see
categories.strategy: Provide information to move them toward Supporter; address specific concerns

categories.description: Opposes the change but open to persuasion
categories.strategy: Understand their specific concerns; address them directly; involve them in solution design
Escalate if they cannot be converted; understand root concern — it may reveal a legitimate flaw

trust_building: Be transparent about what you know and don't know
Follow through on every commitment — no matter how small
Acknowledge stakeholders' expertise — they know their domain better than you
Share credit for good ideas with the stakeholders who contributed them
Communicate bad news early and honestly — never bury it

handling_conflict_between_stakeholders.common_scenario: Two department heads have directly conflicting requirements for the same feature
BA_approach: 1. Listen to both perspectives separately to understand underlying interests (not just stated positions)
2. Find if requirements conflict at the feature level but are compatible at the goal level
3. Facilitate a joint session to surface the shared business goal
4. If truly irreconcilable — escalate to a decision authority (Sponsor, steering committee) with full context

hippo_problem.definition: HiPPO = Highest Paid Person's Opinion. When an executive's preference overrides user research and stakeholder input in requirements decisions.
hippo_problem.risk: Produces solutions that satisfy the executive but not the end users — often fails in adoption
hippo_problem.BA_response: Use data, user research, and objective analysis to support decisions over pure authority. Present options with trade-offs rather than arguing directly.

workshops.definition: Structured, facilitated group sessions to elicit, analyze, and validate requirements from multiple stakeholders simultaneously
facilitation_tips: Set clear objectives: 'By end of this session, we will have agreed on...'
Establish ground rules: one person speaks at a time, all ideas are valid initially
Use visual techniques (whiteboard, sticky notes) to make abstract ideas concrete
Timekeeper and note-taker are essential roles
End with explicit next steps and owners

details.real_world_example: A BA is analyzing requirements for a new HR system. She identifies 7 stakeholder groups: HR managers (High Power, High Interest), employees (Low Power, High Interest), IT (High Power, Medium Interest), Finance (Medium Power, Low Interest), Legal (High Power, Low Interest), external payroll vendor (Medium Power, High Interest), and union representatives (High Power, Medium Interest). She maps all to the power/interest grid and designs different engagement strategies for each. Union representatives — initially resistant — are invited to join two working sessions. Their concern: the new system might replace certain roles. By including them, the BA discovers a legitimate design issue and adjusts the requirements. The union becomes supporters.

exam_tips: Identify stakeholders EARLY and CONTINUOUSLY — new ones emerge throughout the project. High Power + High Interest = Manage Closely. Resistors must be engaged — ignoring them amplifies their resistance. HiPPO is an anti-pattern — support decisions with data. Internal vs external stakeholders need different communication approaches. The BA facilitates stakeholder conflict resolution but escalates irreconcilable conflicts to decision authority.

title: Elicitation — Drawing Out Requirements from Stakeholders
summary: Elicitation is the process of drawing out, exploring, and identifying information needed from stakeholders and other sources to understand the business need and define requirements. The PMI Guide to Business Analysis makes a crucial distinction: elicitation is ACTIVE — it requires deliberate techniques to surface what stakeholders know, feel, and need — including things they cannot easily articulate. Good elicitation is the difference between requirements that reflect real needs and requirements that reflect what stakeholders thought they needed in a meeting.
key_concepts: Elicitation ≠ Documentation: eliciting is the active process; documenting is recording what was elicited
Stated vs Unstated needs: stakeholders often cannot articulate all their needs — techniques help surface them
Tacit knowledge: knowledge stakeholders have but struggle to verbalize — observation is needed
Elicitation planning: choose the right technique for the right context
Confirmation: validate that what was elicited accurately reflects the stakeholder's true need
Multiple techniques: no single technique captures all requirements

business_requirements.definition: High-level statements of goals, objectives, and needs of the organization
business_requirements.example: The organization needs to reduce customer onboarding time from 5 days to 1 day.

stakeholder_requirements.definition: Needs of specific stakeholder groups that must be addressed by the solution
stakeholder_requirements.example: Relationship managers need to see a customer's full history on a single screen.

functional_requirements.definition: Behaviors and capabilities the solution MUST have — what it does
functional_requirements.example: The system shall send an automated welcome email within 5 minutes of account creation.

non_functional_requirements.definition: Quality attributes the solution must exhibit — how well it does what it does

categories.example: System shall process 1,000 transactions per second under peak load
All data at rest shall be encrypted using AES-256
System shall achieve 99.9% uptime (maximum 8.7 hours downtime per year)
New users shall complete onboarding in under 10 minutes without training
System shall support growth from 10,000 to 1,000,000 users without re-architecture
Critical bug fixes shall be deployable within 4 hours of identification

transition_requirements.definition: Temporary requirements needed to move from current state to future state — not permanent
transition_requirements.example: All customer data from the legacy system must be migrated with 100% accuracy within the 8-hour maintenance window.
transition_requirements.key_point: Transition requirements are often FORGOTTEN in requirements gathering — they are critical for successful go-live

constraints.definition: Limitations that restrict solution design choices
examples: Must integrate with existing Oracle ERP — no replacement

interviews.definition: One-on-one or small group conversations to draw out detailed information

structured_vs_unstructured.structured: Pre-defined questions in a fixed order — ensures consistency across interviewees
structured_vs_unstructured.semi_structured: Core questions prepared but allows exploration of unexpected topics — most effective
structured_vs_unstructured.unstructured: Open conversation — useful for exploratory discovery

best_practices: Prepare questions in advance but remain flexible
Ask open-ended questions: 'Tell me about...' rather than 'Do you need...?'
Probe deeper: 'Can you give me an example?', 'What would happen if...?'
Confirm understanding: 'So if I understand correctly, you need...'
interviews.best_for: Complex, sensitive topics; building individual relationships; detailed domain knowledge

workshops.definition: Structured facilitated group sessions with multiple stakeholders

JAD.name: Joint Application Design/Development
JAD.purpose: Intensive workshop where business and IT stakeholders collaboratively design requirements together
JAD.benefit: Reduces back-and-forth review cycles; builds shared ownership

workshops.best_for: Reaching consensus on conflicting requirements; building shared understanding; rapid requirements development

focus_groups.definition: Moderated group discussion with selected stakeholders who share characteristics
focus_groups.vs_workshops: Focus groups gather opinions and reactions; workshops collaboratively build requirements
focus_groups.best_for: Understanding attitudes and perceptions; gathering feedback on proposed solutions; user experience research

surveys_questionnaires.definition: Written set of questions distributed to a large audience
surveys_questionnaires.best_for: Large, geographically distributed stakeholder groups; gathering quantitative data; validating findings from other techniques

observation.definition: Watching stakeholders perform their work in their natural environment to understand actual workflows

types.passive: Observer watches without interacting — 'a fly on the wall'
types.active: Observer participates in the work to directly experience it — job shadowing, apprenticing

observation.why_essential: People often cannot accurately describe what they do — they describe what they THINK they do, or the ideal process, not the actual one
observation.example: BA observes customer service agents for two days. Discovers they maintain a personal spreadsheet of 'workarounds' for system limitations — 23 workarounds exist that no one mentioned in interviews because they are so habitual the agents don't think of them as problems
observation.best_for: Understanding tacit knowledge; discovering unstated needs; process improvement

document_analysis.definition: Reviewing existing documentation to extract requirements and understand the current system
document_analysis.advantage: Fast, non-intrusive — existing artifacts reveal requirements already implemented
document_analysis.best_for: Understanding existing systems; identifying regulatory requirements; discovering constraints early

prototyping.definition: Creating a preliminary model — visual mockup, wireframe, or working prototype — that stakeholders can react to

types.throwaway_prototype: Built quickly to elicit feedback; discarded after requirements are confirmed
types.evolutionary_prototype: Refined iteratively and eventually becomes the actual product (used in agile)

prototyping.why_effective: Seeing is understanding — stakeholders react to concrete prototypes far more accurately than to written descriptions. 'I'll know it when I see it' is real.
prototyping.example: BA shows three wireframe variants of a dashboard to users. Variant A: users say 'great.' Variant B: users say 'this layout makes more sense.' Variant C: users say 'this is exactly what we need — but move the export button here.' Prototype reveals requirements that three rounds of interviews missed.
prototyping.best_for: UX requirements; validating understanding; discovering requirements stakeholders struggle to articulate

brainstorming.definition: Facilitated group technique to generate a large volume of ideas rapidly without evaluation
brainstorming.use_in_BA: Generating solution options; identifying risks; surfacing requirements in early discovery
brainstorming.best_for: Early-stage discovery; creative problem solving; generating options for evaluation

interface_analysis.definition: Identifying and analyzing the points of interaction between the solution and external systems, people, or processes
interface_analysis.why_important: Interface failures are among the most common causes of system implementation problems
interface_analysis.example: New CRM must interface with: legacy billing system (REST API), email marketing platform (webhooks), executive dashboard (read-only data warehouse feed), mobile app (GraphQL API). Each interface has its own requirements.

elicitation_pitfalls.description: Only hearing information that confirms existing assumptions
elicitation_pitfalls.prevention: Ask 'What would tell you this solution is failing?' — surface contrary evidence

elicitation_pitfalls.description: First stakeholder's stated requirement becomes the baseline that others react to — real needs may differ
elicitation_pitfalls.prevention: Use open questions before presenting any options; elicit independently before group sessions

elicitation_pitfalls.description: Collecting 'nice to have' requirements alongside 'must have' — blurring prioritization
elicitation_pitfalls.prevention: Apply MoSCoW or similar prioritization technique during or immediately after elicitation

elicitation_pitfalls.description: Elicitation focuses on 'what the system does' — performance, security, and usability requirements are often forgotten
elicitation_pitfalls.prevention: Use a requirements checklist that explicitly includes non-functional categories

exam_tips: Observation reveals TACIT requirements that interviews miss. Prototyping is best for requirements stakeholders 'can't describe but will recognize.' Different techniques suit different contexts — no single technique is sufficient. Elicitation ≠ documentation — eliciting is the active discovery; recording is what follows. Transition requirements are critical and often forgotten. Non-functional requirements need explicit elicitation — stakeholders rarely volunteer them.

title: Requirements Analysis — Modeling, Validating, and Prioritizing
summary: Requirements Analysis transforms raw elicitation output — notes, ideas, desires — into clear, structured, validated requirements that a development team can act on. The PMI Guide to Business Analysis describes analysis as including modeling (representing requirements visually), verification (checking quality of requirements), validation (checking they reflect real needs), and prioritization (deciding what to build first). Analysis is where ambiguous stakeholder input becomes precise, testable specifications.
key_concepts: Requirements verification: are the requirements well-written? (correct format, clear, complete, consistent)
Requirements validation: do the requirements reflect the actual stakeholder need?
Requirements modeling: visual representations that reveal what text descriptions hide
Decomposition: breaking complex requirements into smaller, analyzable components
Prioritization: deciding the order in which requirements are addressed
Requirements attributes: properties attached to each requirement (priority, source, status, risk)

characteristics_of_good_requirements.description: Well-written requirements are SMART, or more specifically:

characteristics.description: Contains all information needed — no 'TBD' or missing elements
characteristics.bad_example: The system shall process payments quickly.
characteristics.good_example: The system shall process credit card payments and return a success/failure response within 3 seconds for 99% of transactions.

characteristics.bad_example: The system shall provide appropriate error messages.
characteristics.good_example: The system shall display a specific error message for each failure type: 'Invalid card number', 'Insufficient funds', 'Card expired'.

characteristics.bad_example: Req 12: System sends email confirmation. Req 47: System does not send emails to customers.
characteristics.good_example: Requirements reviewed for internal consistency before baseline

characteristics.description: Can be confirmed to be met through testing, inspection, or demonstration
characteristics.good_example: First-time users shall complete the registration process in under 5 minutes without assistance, as measured in usability testing.

characteristics.description: Achievable within known constraints — technically possible, within budget and timeline
characteristics.check: Reviewed with technical team for feasibility before baseline

characteristics.description: Linked to a source (stakeholder, regulation, business need) and forward to design/test
Each requirement has a defined priority level — decisions are made on relative importance

requirements_modeling.definition: Using visual representations to describe requirements — models reveal structure, relationships, and flows that text descriptions obscure

flowchart.description: Shows sequential steps, decision points, and branches in a process

bpmn.name: Business Process Model and Notation
bpmn.description: Standardized notation for representing business processes with defined symbols for swimlanes, gateways, events
bpmn.use: Formal process documentation; communicating processes to both business and technical stakeholders

swim_lane_diagram.description: Flowchart organized by responsible party (swim lanes show who does what)
swim_lane_diagram.use: Clarifying handoff points between roles or systems — often reveals where handoff delays occur

use_cases.definition: Narrative description of how an actor (user or system) interacts with the system to achieve a goal
components: Actor: who or what interacts with the system
Goal: what the actor wants to achieve
Preconditions: what must be true before the use case can start
Main success scenario: the normal flow of events
Alternative flows: variations from the main flow
Exception flows: error conditions and system responses
Postconditions: what is true after the use case completes

example_structure.goal: Submit an expense report for reimbursement
example_structure.preconditions: Employee is logged in; expense receipts have been uploaded
main_flow: Employee enters report details (date range, purpose)
Employee adds line items by selecting from uploaded receipts
System validates all required fields and categories
System sends report to employee's manager for approval
System confirms submission with email to employee
example_structure.alternative_flow: If manager is unavailable (>5 business days), system escalates to skip-level manager
example_structure.exception_flow: If a receipt is missing for a line item over $50, system blocks submission and displays specific error

vs_user_stories.use_cases: More detailed; prescribe the full interaction sequence; better for complex functional requirements
vs_user_stories.user_stories: Brief; focus on user value; better for agile iterative development

entity_relationship_diagram.description: Shows data entities, their attributes, and relationships between entities
entity_relationship_diagram.use: Defining data requirements; communicating with database designers
entity_relationship_diagram.example: Customer (CustomerID, Name, Email) — Places → Order (OrderID, Date, Total) — Contains → Product (ProductID, Name, Price)

data_flow_diagram.description: Shows how data moves through a system — processes, data stores, external entities, and data flows
data_flow_diagram.use: Understanding information flows; identifying data requirements

state_diagram.description: Shows the different states an object can be in and the transitions between states
state_diagram.use: Complex business objects with lifecycle states
state_diagram.example: Order states: Created → Submitted → Approved → Fulfilled → Cancelled. Each transition has trigger conditions.

moscow.name: MoSCoW
moscow.description: Categorizes requirements into Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have this time
moscow.use_when: Scoping a release or sprint; communicating priority to stakeholders
rules: Must have items: project fails without them
Should have items: important but workarounds exist temporarily
Could have items: nice to have if time and budget permit
Won't have this time: explicitly out of scope for this release (may be future)

value_vs_effort.description: 2x2 matrix plotting each requirement by business value (Y) and implementation effort (X)

quadrants.action: Fill-in items — do if capacity permits
Money pits — avoid or defer indefinitely

kano_model.description: Categorizes features by their impact on customer satisfaction

categories.description: Expected by default — their absence causes dissatisfaction but their presence is taken for granted
categories.example: A banking app must show account balance — users expect it; it's not a differentiator

categories.description: More is better — linearly increases satisfaction
categories.example: Faster transaction processing → proportionally higher satisfaction

categories.description: Unexpected features that delight customers when present but don't dissatisfy when absent
categories.example: Banking app proactively alerts user of unusual spending patterns — unexpected and delightful

categories.description: Neither presence nor absence affects satisfaction
categories.example: Technical architecture choices invisible to users

categories.description: Presence causes dissatisfaction for some users
categories.example: Excessive notifications — many users turn them off

kano_model.use_when: Product strategy decisions; differentiating features for competitive advantage

wsjf.name: Weighted Shortest Job First
wsjf.formula: WSJF = Cost of Delay / Job Size
wsjf.use_when: Prioritizing large program backlogs; balancing value, urgency, and effort
wsjf.benefit: Prevents high-effort, high-value items from always being displaced by low-effort items

verification.question: Are we building requirements CORRECTLY?
verification.who: BA and technical team — internal quality check

validation.question: Are we building the RIGHT requirements?
validation.when: After requirements are documented; before development begins

outputs: Requirements models (use cases, process flows, data models)
exam_tips: Verification = quality of the requirement (is it well-written?). Validation = accuracy of the requirement (does it reflect the real need?). Both are necessary. A testable requirement has specific, measurable criteria — 'fast' is not testable; 'under 3 seconds for 99% of transactions' is. Non-functional requirements are just as binding as functional ones. MoSCoW for scoping; Kano for product differentiation; WSJF for program-level prioritization.

title: Requirements Traceability — Tracking Requirements Through the Lifecycle
summary: Requirements Traceability is the ability to track a requirement from its origin through its implementation and testing, and to verify that it has been fully satisfied. The PMI Guide to Business Analysis defines traceability as essential for managing requirements change, ensuring completeness, demonstrating regulatory compliance, and conducting impact analysis when changes are requested. The Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM) is the primary tool.
key_concepts: Traceability Matrix (RTM): document linking requirements to their source and to design, development, and test artifacts
Forward traceability: requirement → design → build → test (ensures all requirements are implemented and tested)
Backward traceability: test → build → requirement → business need (ensures nothing built lacks justification)
Bidirectional traceability: both forward and backward — most complete view
Impact analysis: when a requirement changes, identify all affected design, code, and test artifacts
Coverage analysis: identify requirements without corresponding test cases (testing gap)

details.definition: Requirements Traceability is the ability to describe and follow the life of a requirement in both a forward and backward direction — from origin through development and testing to delivery. It ensures requirements are not lost, that all requirements are implemented, and that all implementation can be justified.

rtm_explained.definition: A table linking requirements to their business justification, design specifications, development components, and test cases

example_row.description: System shall send email confirmation within 5 minutes of order placement
example_row.source: Customer satisfaction survey — 73% of customers want confirmation

forward_traceability.direction: Business Need → Requirement → Design → Code → Test Case → Test Result
forward_traceability.purpose: Verify that every requirement is implemented and tested
forward_traceability.gap_detection: A requirement with no corresponding test case is a testing gap — risk of unverified functionality

backward_traceability.direction: Test Case → Code → Design → Requirement → Business Need
backward_traceability.purpose: Verify that everything built can be justified by a requirement
backward_traceability.gap_detection: Code with no corresponding requirement may be gold plating or unauthorized scope

bidirectional.description: Most complete view — enables full impact analysis in either direction
bidirectional.use_when: Regulated industries, high-assurance systems, compliance demonstration

impact_analysis.definition: Using the traceability matrix to understand the full impact of a proposed change to a requirement
process: 1. Identify the requirement proposed for change
2. Trace forward: what design specifications reference this requirement?
3. What code components implement those specifications?
4. What test cases verify that code?
5. Identify all affected items — this is the impact of the change
6. Estimate the effort to update all affected items
7. Present impact analysis to decision-maker (CCB or PO)
impact_analysis.real_value: Without traceability, a 'small' requirement change cascades unexpectedly into expensive rework. With traceability, the BA can say: 'This change affects 3 design documents, 7 code modules, and 12 test cases — estimate 3 weeks of effort.'

traceability_in_agile.challenge: Traditional RTM is heavyweight — conflicts with agile principle of minimal documentation
agile_approach: User stories in the Product Backlog serve as lightweight requirements
Acceptance criteria are the implicit test trace
Definition of Done includes automated test coverage — implicit traceability
Many agile teams use lightweight tagging (story ID in commit messages and test names) for automation-friendly traceability
traceability_in_agile.regulated_agile: In regulated industries using agile, a lightweight RTM is maintained — story ID → regulatory requirement → automated test. Sufficient for audit with much less overhead than traditional RTM.

traceability_use_cases.example: FDA requires demonstration that every safety requirement in the specification has been tested and verified. RTM provides the audit trail.
Sponsor asks: 'Did we build everything we agreed to?' RTM shows all requirements and their test pass status.
Customer asks to change a data field format. RTM immediately shows 4 other requirements reference this field, 12 screens display it, and 8 reports use it.
Before UAT, QA manager reviews RTM. 15 requirements have no corresponding test case — these are added to the test plan.

methods_tools: Requirements Management Tools (JIRA, Azure DevOps, IBM DOORS)
exam_tips: RTM links requirements from business need through design, development, and testing. Forward traceability = all requirements implemented and tested. Backward traceability = all code justified by requirements. Bidirectional = both. Impact analysis uses RTM to quantify the effect of a change before approving it. In Agile, story IDs + automated tests provide lightweight traceability. The RTM is essential for regulatory compliance demonstration.

title: Solution Evaluation — Assessing Whether the Solution Delivers Value
summary: Solution Evaluation is the BA knowledge area focused on assessing solutions — both during development and after delivery — to determine whether they deliver the intended business value. The PMI Guide to Business Analysis emphasizes that delivery of outputs (features, deliverables) does not equal realization of value. Solution Evaluation closes the loop: was the right problem solved? Did the solution work? What improvements are needed?
key_concepts: Solution evaluation during development: validate that the solution being built will meet needs before delivery
Solution evaluation after delivery: measure whether the solution actually delivered the promised value
Acceptance criteria: pre-defined conditions that must be met for the solution to be accepted
User Acceptance Testing (UAT): stakeholders validate the solution against real-world needs
Business value measurement: quantifying whether the business benefits promised in the business case were realized
Post-implementation review: structured assessment after go-live to capture lessons learned

details.definition: Solution Evaluation encompasses the activities used to assess the performance of and value delivered by a solution, identify issues or problems with the solution, and determine whether a solution still meets the business need over time.

during_initiation.focus: Will the proposed solution actually solve the problem? Is it viable?

during_development.activity: Validate that what is being built aligns with requirements
during_development.focus: Are we building the right thing? Are we building it correctly?

before_release.focus: Does the solution meet real user needs in real conditions?

after_release.focus: Did the solution deliver the promised business value?

acceptance_criteria.definition: Specific conditions that a deliverable must satisfy to be accepted by the sponsor, product owner, or customer
characteristics: Defined BEFORE development begins — not after
Testable — a tester can verify pass/fail without ambiguity
Agreed upon by all parties before development

example.ac_1: Given a customer completes checkout, When payment is processed successfully, Then the customer receives an email confirmation within 5 minutes
